CANADIAN FORCES-SEPARATION ALLOWANCES TO WIVES OF PROFESSIONAL ENLISTED MEN, CARRYING ON PRIVATE PRACTICE
speechtext:
1.	Is separation allowance paid to wives of any enlisted men who besides their military duties carry on a private practice in their civilian profession?
2.	If so, in what professions and how many in each?

subtopic: CANADIAN FORCES-SEPARATION ALLOWANCES TO WIVES OF PROFESSIONAL ENLISTED MEN, CARRYING ON PRIVATE PRACTICE
speechtext:
1.	(a) There is no record of any enlisted men on active service who, besides their military duties, carry on a private practice in their civilian professions.
(b) In so far as officers are concerned, there are no records to show that any officers on active service practise a private profession in addition to their military duties. Certain medical officers who are members of the reserve army are called up from time to time for periodic employment with standing medical boards and the wives of such officers are entitled to receive dependents' allowance for the number of days in eaclh month in which t'heir husbands perform military duties. These officers are not members of the active forces and are, in fact, civilian practitioners. It is reasonable, therefore, to expect that they
would continue to maintain their private practices during those 'hours when not actually employed on military duties.
2.	See answer to question No. 1.

speechtext:
Last night I received a letter franked by the Clerk of the House. Inclosed in it was -a tetter addressed to "Members of Parliament." This letter had -been opened, and apparently it was decided to send it to me by reason of the -fact that the writer lives in -my constituency. I wish to ask a question based npon this letter, and as it is very short I will read it and then -address my question to the Minister of Agriculture. The letter reads:
Members of Parliament,
Ottawa.
Dear Sirs-
Why isn't the wheat insurance money paid? There are some people Who h-ave received cheques but there are many who have not, and wha-t d-o you think we are living on in the meantime? It should be paid. You don't seem
Prairie Farm Assistance

to realize what trouble and havoc is being caused, but I oould tell you. I wish we of the western prairies could tell you face to face.
Yours truly,
Mrs. Donald Sutherland
In view of the fact that many western members have received similar letters, what is holding up the payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act? Secondly, will it 'be 'possible after March 1 to include the second payment with the first where the first payment has not already been made?

speechtext: Last evening an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) to which exception was taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Does any hon. member wish to speak to the point of order raised?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Last evening, just before six
o'clock, and after the hon. member for Lake Centre had moved his amendment, the Prime Minister raised a point of order, submitting that the amendment was out of order. He further added, at page 839 of Hansard:
... I raise the point now in order that your honour may have an opportunity to consider the matter.
Then he briefly stated the point of order:
The amendment tends to amend the bill, which I do not think is right, and the amendment does not object to the principle of the bill.
In that connection, as I recall it, the right hon. gentleman cited one of the rules of this house, though that is not incorporated in the objection which he made. If I apprehend his position aright, however, it was standing order 75 to which he alluded. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: 'Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Standing order 75 appears at page 216, of Beauchesne and reads:
Every public bill shall be read twice in the house before committal or amendment.
I have a legal argument to make; it may take me some little time, and I crave the indulgence of the house while I do so. I should like to say that I have not had the opportunity to prepare a thorough brief on the matter, but what I have I should like to give to the house without interruption, if I may.
I have just read standing order 75, and I ask hon. members to note the date: 1867. Now
I propose to read the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre, appearing at page S38 of Hansard
That the bill be not now read a second time but that this house is of the opinion that the use of the powers conferred thereby be restricted to the submission thereunder of one plebiscite only.
Even at first blush, on reading standing order 75, I submit there is nothing in 'this amendment which is contrary to the provisions of that order, unless something is read into it. But we have been able to find at least four cases since 1867 where what is now proposed has been done in parliament. I want to cite a number of authorities. The first to which I direct Your Honour's attention is a ruling given by the Speaker of the British House of Commons on the Anglo-German agreement bill, in wihiclh it was laid down in Hansard debates, 1890, third series, 347, at page 743:
It is competent for any hon. member to move a resolution superseding the motion for the second reading, but it is not competent to add words to the motion "that the bill be now read a second time."
That is a statement of principle, and that is what is sought to be done here. The amendment offered by the hon. member for Lake Centre does not propose to add to the motion that the bill be now read a second time. It proposes to supersede that motion entirely. I therefore submit that under the rule which I have quoted it is competent for him to move such a motion.
The amendment in question proposes that the bill be not now read a second time, and then proceeds to assert a principle. The important word in the first part of the amendment is the word "now", where it is stated that it be not now read a second time. That does not mean "never". The amendment does not mean that the bill will never be read a second time. If the proposed amendment is passed in the affirmative the Secretary of State would be entirely within his rights to move again without notice the main motion, that the bill be now read a second time. That is clear from the statement appearing in May, thirteenth edition, page 392, as follows:
It must be borne in mind, however, that the resolution, if agreed to-
And in this instance I would use the word "amendment",-
-does not arrest the progress of the bill, the second reading of which may be moved on another occasion. The effect of such an amendment is merely 'to supersede the question for now reading the bill a second time; and the

Plebiscite Act-Point of Order
bill is left in the same position as if the question for now reading the bill a second time had been simply negatived or superseded by the previous question.
The result is that if the amendment is carried1 in the affirmative the bill may, at a later stage, be read the second time; but in the meantime the house will have asserted an important principle in connection with the operation of the bill, namely,-
-that 'this house is of the opinion that the use of the powers conferred thereby be restricted to the submission thereunder of one plebiscite only.
These are the words of the amendment. I could quote to Your Honour a large number of precedents, both in the British House of Commons and in this house, showing that it is possible for an amendment to be made on the second reading of a bill, provided that such amendment does not seek to add words to the motion that the bill be now read a second time, but on the contrary proposes to supersede it.
At pages 390 and 391 of May, thirteenth edition, this is made quite clear.

The question is not germane to the point at issue, and I do not propose to answer it. I am dealing with a very technical question of parliamentary law and practice, and notwithstanding the erudition of which I know the bon. member is possessed, I would ask him to possess his soul in patience. I do not mean anything offensive in that, but I must point out that in my opinion the interruption was not pertinent.
When the hon. member spoke I was proceeding to refer Your Honour to pages 390 and 391 of May, thirteenth edition; and with your permission I shall read this citation, one which I believe makes my submission quite clear;
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move, as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from the principles, policy or provisions of the bill; or expressing opinions

as to any circumstances connected with its introduction or prosecution; or otherwise opposed to its progress; or seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees, commissioners, the production of papers or other evidence, or, in the Lords, the opinions of the judges.
On page 391 it is stated that an amendment must not "attach conditions to the second reading of the bill". This merely means that an amendment must not seek to add words to the motion "that the bill now be read a second time", but that if it supersedes the motion entirely and asserts a principle, it is entirely in order.

When
was that?

speechtext:
It was on
April 24, 1934. The record will be found at page 271 of the Journals of the House, and if it is necessary to emphasize the authority, particularly to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, I would say that the ruling on that occasion was given by his friend and my friend the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) when he was occupying the chair of the speakership of this house. I quote from page 271:
The order being read for resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Air. Weir (Atelfort), for the second reading of Bill No. 51, An Act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of national products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith, and the proposed motion of Air. Alackenzie King in amendment thereto;
And a point of order having been raised;

Plebiscite Act-Point of Order
Then comes the quotation of Mr. Speaker's ruling:
Mr. Speaker: "It having been moved that Bill 51, An Act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade and to make further provision in connection therewith, be now read a second time, the Right Horn Mr. Mackenzie King moved in amendment: 'That all the words after the first word "That" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
this house, while prepared to support legislation for assisting the orderly marketing of natural products, is unalterably opposed to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation, and which confers upon a minister of the crown, and upon the governor in council unprecedented authority and unusual powers to restrict production, and interprovincial, inter-imperial and foreign trade as regards both exports and imports, as well as other autocratic powers.'
"Hon. Mr. Stevens raised the point of order as to whether the said amendment is in order inasmuch as it constitutes what might be termed a declaration of policy instead of offering reasons why consideration of the bill should not be proceeded with or should be postponed or proposing something else germane to the actual motion before the house.
"The Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King in moving the amendment quoted paragraph 755 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, which paragraph is published as a quotation from May, 13th Edition at page 390, which is repeated by Bourinot at page 509:
" 'It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from the principles, policy or provisions of the bill.'
"This rule is subject to certain limitations.
His Honour the Speaker continues:
If the right hon. member had continued to quote from May, he would have found the following reference to an amendment to a motion for second reading of a bill-'Nor may such an amendment deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee.'
That is from May, thirteenth edition, page 91, and the precedent as cited in May in .support of this from 188 Parliamentary Debates, 4th series, column 76, "The Education (Scotland) Bill" reads:
"'Mr. Speaker:	I have to rule that the
amendment standing in the name of the hon. member for Glasgow and Aberdeen universities -to the effect that the house while welcoming educational legislation for Scotland regrets that the present measure does not propose change in the educational areas, which is urgently required in the interests of efficient administration-is not technically in order, because it does not
challenge the principle of the bill. The question raised can be decided by an amendment to the bill itself. If the hon. member wants to object to the second reading, he should move that the bill be read this day six months.'
Then His Honour the Speaker continued with his ruling:
"The amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition does not challenge the principle of Bill 51, and it anticipates the committee stage. It declares that the 'house is prepared to support legislation for assisting the orderly marketing of natural products' and the bill is intituled:	'An Act to improve the
methods and practices of marketing of natural products.' There is so much similarity between those two propositions that one cannot be moved as a reason to reject the second reading of a bill enunciating the other. The bill deals with powers and methods which may be altered in committee.
"The objection to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation can be decided by amendments when the committee of the whole is considering section 3 of the bill which establishes the Dominion marketing board and section 4 which defines the powers of the board. The action to be taken by the governor in council and the minister in administering the act is described in almost every section of the bill and may be strengthened or weakened by amendment when the bill is in committee.
"The objections raised in the proposed amendment cannot be looked upon as reasons why bill 51 should not now be proceeded with and, moreover, they may be considered after the bill has been read a second time.
"For these reasons, I find the proposed amendment to be out of order."
I think, Mr. Speaker, you will agree and that hon. members will also agree that the parallel is perfect with respect to the relevancy of the amendment which I had sought to introduce in 1934, and which was ruled out of order, and the amendment which the hon. member for Lake Centre has introduced, and which I believe will also be ruled out of order.

speechtext:
In the present debate on the second reading of Bill No. 10, "An Act respecting the taking of a plebiscite in every electoral district in Canada and the taking 
of the votes at such plebiscite of Canadian service voters stationed within and without Canada," Mr. Diefenbaker moved an: amendment:
That the bill be not read a second time but that this house is of the opinion that the use of the powers conferred thereby be restricted to the submission thereunder of one plebiscite only.
I have listened very carefully to the cases which were cited by the leader of the opposition, but I did not find in any of them, that they related to amendments-I include those instances which were discussed in the British House of Commons and also in our own- which were not dealing with the principle of a bill. I have had occasion to see and to read the cases which were cited by the Prime Minister, and I think they are on all fours and entirely apposite to the position we are in to-day.
In Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, standing order 75, page 217, citation number 753, it is stated:
The second reading of a bill is that stage when it is proper to enter into a discussion and propose a motion relative to the principle of the measure.
It is very necessary to state that it is the principle of the measure which is being discussed on the second reading. That is so clear and so distinct that there can be no misunderstanding of the intention of that citation. Further, citation 755 of standing order 75 states:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution; or otherwise opposed to its progress; or seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees, commissioners, the production of papers or other evidence or the opinion of judges.
And there is a reference to May, thirteenth edition, page 357, and Bourinot, fourth edition, page 509.
A motion opposing the second reading of a bill must not anticipate amendments which may be moved in committee, and alterations which may be effected by amending the clauses of the bill cannot be moved in the second reading, as decided by the Speaker in the two cases quoted by the Prime Minister. I may point out that in the latter case, that of the 24th April, 1934, a division took place on an appeal from the Speaker's decision, and this house sustained the Speaker in ruling the amendment out of order.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Veniot
The amendment now moved does not challenge the principle of the bill; in fact it agrees with the principle of the bill for the taking of a plebiscite; and I would again read the terms of the amendment:
That the bill be not now read a second time but that this house is of the opinion that the use of the powers conferred thereby be restricted to the submission thereunder of one plebiscite only.
Therefore in the amendment there is an agreement with the principle of the bill, namely, the taking of a plebiscite, but it states that the powers therein conferred should be restricted to the submission thereunder of one plebiscite only. The amendment also anticipates the committee stage of the bill; and the hon. member would serve his purpose by moving amendments to those clauses in committee on the bill.
For these reasons I rule the amendment out of order.

speechtext:
As the
-first member on this side of the house to take part in to-day's debate, I wish to extend congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon his statesmanlike and masterful address of yesterday, wherein he expressed without equivocation his views and those of his associates in the cabinet on the subject under debate at the present time. He clarified many points, and expressed his continued desire to maintain throughout the nation peace and harmony-a condition which is just as important to-day as the manufacturing of tanks and guns. What a difference there would be in the situation of Canada if we had had as head of the government a man whose character was synonymous with intolerance, narrowness of views, rapier-like thrusts, and vituperation. I feel certain that long ago this country would have been subjected to a great number of disturbances, perhaps to the point of riot and revolution, if certain ideas which are advocated to-day had been carried out sooner. With all the fervour in my heart I say, let Canada thank the Almighty for having at its head today a man of the steadfastness, the equanimity and the balance of the present Prime Minister of Canada.
Before approaching the subjects with which I desire to deal, I should like to take a minute or two to consider certain statements made yesterday by the brilliant young member -for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), in which he upbraided the cabinet for what he termed its abuse of government by order in council. I wish to refer to historical facts of the last war as contained in a book which I have already
mentioned, "The Crisis of Quebec, 1914-18," by E. H. Armstrong, page 54, in which it is stated:
The Canadian War Book, analogous to the British one, provided not only for the eventual raising of troops, but also for the issuance of orders in council and proclamations dealing with such wartime measures as the censorship of cables and the prohibition of certain exports.
On page 65:
What came to be known in 1918 as'order in council government, comprising such unpopular measures as the wholesale cancellation of draft exemptions by >a mere decree of the governor general in council, was legalized by the wide powers granted under the War Measures Act of 1914. At that time it met with scarcely any opposition.
On page 232, referring to the same subject:
. . . as time went on land dissatisfaction with the Military service Act, the cancellation of exemptions, and the so-called "order in council government" pervaded the dominion and led to riots elsewhere, the Quebec riots took on much less of a distinctively Freneh-Ganadian character and were seen to be parts of a nation-wide	movement of resistance to
conscription.
And on page 236 the author, referring to this same subject of orders in council, says:
There were many members, English as well as Freneh-Canadians, who protested against the government's use of the order in council to enforce its wishes, especially in the administration of military service. There was considerable feeling that legislation by order in council constituted an abuse of the executive power, being no more nor less than government by ordinance issued by the federal cabinet.
The Prime Minister, when he rose to uphold the government's mode of action in the Quebec riots, immediately defended the use of the order in council. He stated that the right to use this form of legislation had been granted very extensively by the War Measures Act of 1914, that in the war emergencies it .was often necessary to act quickly, and that the delay of an appeal to parliament might on occasion be disastrous.
So much for that. I now come to the theme of my discourse.
Since the beginning of this session, I have received, as no doubt many other hon. members have, letters requesting information concerning the definite object of the plebiscite. Some view the measure as containing the germ of conscription; others expect conscription to follow immediately on the conclusion of the plebiscite. So far as I can see, the official opposition seem to entertain the wishful hope that this will take place, in order to bring about what they conceive as the ideal measure of an all-out war effort. Others -and to this group I belong-see in the plebiscite an indication of the desire of the government, in case the nation is confronted with a supreme danger, to be free by the
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Veniot

will of the people to take whatever measures it deems necessary in order to protect the nation and the allied cause, even if we must have recourse to a certain measure of conscription for overseas.
What I cannot conceive is that this government, even if we arrive at the point where the nation is confronted with supreme danger, would endeavour to enforce conscription, any measure >of conscription, in the odious way in which it was carried out in 1917, for instance, when troops from Ontario were sent into the province of Quebec to track down evaders; and the same condition of affairs occurred in New Brunswick. I have already expressed myself as willing to accept a certain measure of compulsion for service overseas, provided that I can be shown the absolute failure of voluntary enlistment. But I wish to remind the house and the government that it is a very dangerous policy to ask a nation or a people to make the supreme sacrifice until this nation or people is convinced of the need for such supreme sacrifice. In my estimation the hour has not yet arrived when such a necessity exists. We have before us the gigantic task of educating our people as to the seriousness of the situation. You, sir, and I, see the danger; but the great majority of the people do not entertain the same view. For reasons which already have been submitted to this house I repeat that this country is far from being ripe for the acceptance of any form of compulsion for overseas service. In this opinion may I say that I have the concurrence of a newspaper which is not in great favour with the opposition party, but which nevertheless expresses practically the same view; I refer to the Winnipeg Free Press. In a recent editorial it stated:
The Free Press is published a long way from the province of Quebec, but it knew that the state of opinion in that province was such that any attempt to impose conscription for overseas service by arbitrary, high-handed courses would result in an explosion that would destroy for the duration of the w~ar, and for long after, national unity in Canada. It therefore opposed this policy of coercion and urged more politic and moderate measures. That the Free Press was right in its estimate of the state of public opinion in Quebec can no longer be denied.
May 1 continue a quotation from this same editorial indicating the trend in favour of imposing conscription on Canada, in spite of the fact that the country is not ripe for such a measure. The editorial continues:
Their hope-
The hope of the Toronto junta which decided some four months ago that they would take charge of the affairs of Canada-
[DOT]-was that by exploiting demands for national government and for conscription, they could

disrupt the dominion government; drive Mr. King from the premiership; make it impossible-for the French ministers to remain in office; make possible the coming into office of a government which would be exclusively Englishspeaking with a parliamentary support similarly exclusive. This may look like a wild statement, but nevertheless it is true. The French were to be put in their place; a government more agreeable to reactionaries in financial and political circles was to come into office; there was to be considerably less "truck and trade with the Yankees". In short the clock was to be put back and a government created with policies that, would meet with the approval of all those folk who agree with the contributor of the current issue of Saturday Night, who tells us that "the essence of French-Canadian outlook" is "an unwillingness to concede the battle of the plains of Abraham". It is startling that such unspeakable idiocy should command some measure of support; but unfortunately it does. A quite prominent member of the Toronto group has given expression to this very view in recent years.
I ask the leader of the opposition what he thinks of such dangerous and provocative utterances coming from some of his supporters in the holy city. Is it not a strange coincidence that the intensification of the clamour for conscription occurred last fall precisely at- the moment when it became known that the bulwark against conscription, that giant Canadian statesman, the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, was about to disappear from the political scene? Is it not a coincidence that it happened when it was definitely realized that his mighty voice defending Canadian liberties and privileges was about to be silenced by the pall of death? His passing was the signal, as everyone knows, of a sudden blitzkrieg of forces aimed at splitting the Liberal party by renewing with accrued vigour the sudden cry for conscription which reached even the ranks of the Liberal party.
Not so very long ago I was castigated for having made what was termed a most dangerous speech, when I characterized conscription as having been transformed into a racial issue. No doubt the ire of the hon. gentleman who so characterized me was aroused by the fact that I placed this child on the doorstep of the Conservative party which directed the affairs of Canada in 1917. Hon. members from New Brunswick, although we have personal regard for the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) as a gentleman, know his habit of viewing certain questions by the light of a small tallow candle instead of by the radiance of God's own sunshine. At the first opportunity he tried to convey to certain sections of this country the idea that I entertained the determination to make conscription a racial issue.
I wish to state that there was no such determination on my part. That determination was

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Veniot
made by the fathers of conscription, who conceived that child in 1917 and fostered it ever since. That determination was made rather by the gentlemen from Toronto to whom the Winnipeg Free Press referred in the editorial I quoted a few minutes ago. I wonder if the leader of the opposition listened carefully yesterday to tlhe quotations made by the Prime Minister from speeches delivered in this house by the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, by the leader of the opposition in March, 1939, and by these gentlemen during the last campaign. I wondered also, as the Prime Minister said yesterday, why the hon. gentleman did not denounce the words of his leader of that time as being dangerous, because ibis utterances then dealt with the racial nature of conscription, the dangerous elements which it contained; and the possibility that it would develop strife and division throughout the dominion.
Of course I realize with regret that the 'hon. gentleman's knowledge of French does not permit him to understand all the speeches made by my fellow Canadians from the province of Quebec concerning the question of conscription. I realize also that he may not have had time at his disposal to read the English translations of those speeches which appeared in Hansard; and I realize also that he may not have time in the next two or three years to read certain books which treat very forcefully this same question of conscription, and throw a great deal of light on the nature of the issue.
All the speeches and books I have mentioned contain the same thoughts that have been expressed in this house in recent days, except that they have been couched in different language. My crime has been that of stripping conscription of the hypocrisy with which it has been surrounded for the past twenty-five years; of pulling it out of the odious pussyfooting and beating around the bush to which it has been subjected by, I may say, all political parties since the last war. Let us call things by their true names. A rose by any other name still smells as sweet. Dynamite by any other appellation contains just as much destructive power. Pussyfooting about conscription is just as dangerous as so many tons of TNT under the foundations of national unity in this country. It is potentially fraught with just as great disaster and dissension when it is called by the sweet sounding name of selective service for overseas.
To explain my position on this issue may I be permitted, though it is rather disagreeable to me to do so, to speak of my background. Within the last two weeks I have been pointed out as a French fanatic, though I regret to use that term. Let me say that my father,
one time premier of New Brunswick, and one time postmaster general in this House of Commons, devoted his entire life, as every hon. member of this house knows, to fostering and promoting bonne entente, harmony and union between the two great races of this country. I will admit that between my father and the leader of the opposition there did exist political animosity; but I also know, as the hon. gentleman knows, that there existed between them a certain amount of personal friendship.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
And there is that same personal friendship between us at the present time. We may hold different political opinions, but as individuals we leave those things aside, no matter what bitter enemies we may be in politics. My father endeavoured to instil into me and the other members of the family that same desire to foster a better feeling between the two races. As a physician and a public man I have endeavoured in every way to follow in my father's footsteps in that regard. The dearest and truest friends I have, in and -out of my profession, are of English-speaking descent, and the great majority of them are Protestants. I can also say that in my active professional practice the great majority of my clients were nonCatholics, and the same thing applies to my large drug business in the town of Bathurst. My three daughters-I am going all the way- were educated and received their university degrees at an English institution in the city of Halifax. Why? Because I desired them to have the broad English view as well as the French view, so that they might be better Canadians. My only son is a third year medical student, not at the French university of Laval, for which I have a great deal of respect, nor at the university of Montreal, but at the English Protestant Dalhousie university, for the same reason.
I ask this house: Is such a background conducive to fanatical expressions in this house with regard to race? I deny that in toto. My sole endeavour has been and will continue to be to enlighten my fellow-Canadians as much as I possibly can as to the factual, historical, political and racial significance of conscription as I have studied the question, and to point out the explosive dangers to the nation of any such measure. I realize that I have not much time at my disposal, though I did not take note of the time I started to speak; but I propose to indicate certain facts concerning conscription which are found in a book which I think it very important that every hon. member of
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Veniot

this house should read, a book to which I referred a few moments ago. This book contains all the historical facts, for which all the references are indicated. It was written by a person who lives outside Canada, a former New Yorker but now a Washingtonian. That may foe disagreeable to some hon. members in this house who formerly preached the slogan, "No truck or trade with the United States." The author of this book is a disinterested outsider who has no axe to grind for the province of Quebec or any other province of this dominion; for eonscriptionists or anti-conscriptionists; a person who spent six months practically without interruption in the library of this House of Commons, as can be verified by consulting our librarians, and in the archives of the government, gathering material for this very valuable work.
The first chapter of this book is concerned with the roots of French-Canadianismit indicates the struggles which took place from the conquest of New France by England up to the beginning of the last war. The second chapter deals with the trials of French-Canadian nationality. The third chapter indicates French-Canadian nationalism at the outbreak of the war. The fourth and fifth chapters, which should interest this house, show the united Canada of 1914 and the revival of national conflict with French Canada on the defensive in 1916. May I be permitted, as time allows, to read a few quotations from this work, the first from page 55:
Britain entered the war on August 4. . . On the same day the governor general telegraphed the king that "Canada stands united from the Pacific to the Atlantic in her determination to uphold the honour and traditions of our empire."
Then, in the next paragraph:
The most striking phenomenon in the first months of the war was the practical unanimity of all shades of Canadian opinion.
And a few lines further down:
But in 1914 Canadians of both races and all religions were bound in a sort of union sacrie * . . throughout the length and breadth of the province of Quebec there were demonstrations of popular acclaim for the cause of Britain and her allies.
And on page 56:
In Quebec, the old capital of Canada, there were enthusiastic pro-war demonstrations in which English, Irish, and French Canadians joined.
And in the next paragraph:
With a unanimity that is all the more striking when the bitter divisions of the later years of the war are considered, the representatives of every shade of French-Canadian political opinion, Liberals, Conservatives and even Nationalists seemed to vie with each other in expressions of enthusiasm for the allied
[Mr. Veniot.l
cause and for Canadian participation. . . . From the very beginning of the European conflict, the official leader of French-Canadian thought-
Sir Wilfrid Laurier-
-ranged himself on the side of an active Canadian participation in the war.
Then, on page 57:
Laurier appealed to his own countrymen in eloquent terms to enlist.
And on page 58:
That the Catholic leaders did not at this time shirk from envisaging a whole-hearted Canadian cooperation in the empire's war effort is proved by Archbishop Bruchesi's supplementary statement-
Then the statement follows. And further:
Laurier . . . admonished the French Canadians among the soldiers to remember that "England has protected our liberties and our faith. Under her flag we have found peace, and now in appreciation of what England has done, you go as French Canadians to do your utmost to keep the Union Jack flying in honour to the breeze."
And at page 59:
Pastoral letters . . . have been at times of great influence in keeping the French Canadians in the path of obedience and loyalty to the mother country.
And further down the page:
The bishops did not hesitate to assert that because England was engaged in the war, it was clear that the fate of all parts of the empire was linked to the success of her arms.
I could go on quoting endlessly to show that in those days the most perfect harmony and unity existed among Canadians of all races, all creeds and all nationalities.
Then, at page 64:
On the Liberal as much as on the Conservative side of the House of Commons it seemed to be the consensus of opinion that the government should be given carte blanche to help win the war.
And at page 67:
There was absolutely no difference of opinion on the righteousness of the cause of the allies or of the necessity of Canada's coming to the help of the mother country in the great emergency. *
I now pass to the next chapter, in order to save time. At page S3 I find this:
It was only natural that there arose at that time a widely supported movement for the formation of a battalion to be exclusively composed of French Canadians.
There was an insistent demand for a French-Canadian unit.
French Canadians were sometimes assigned to units predominantly English-speaking and protestant, where the atmosphere was decidedly uncongenial to them.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Homuth
And further down:
They were further annoyed by the lack of French-Canadian instructors and by the refusal of the authorities to allow more than one French-Canadian company under French-Canadian officers in the first contingent. . . The consequent desire for a unit in which French Canadians would be assured of a sympathetic milieu for the free exercise of their religion and customs was very strong. Meanwhile French-Canadian leaders of both parties had given their support to the scheme for a French-Canadian unit. . . .
The consequent authorization on September 30 for the formation of a battalion to be known as the Royal 22nd French Canadians was hailed with patriotic satisfaction throughout the province of Quebec. Conservative and Liberal editors of rural and city newspapers alike united in cordial approval of the scheme. . . .
With the formation of a French-Canadian battalion and the recruiting campaign, of which the Parc Sohmer meeting was an outstanding event, it seemed that French Canada's war effort had been given exactly the proper impetus and that it would only be necessary to keep it going.
Immediately following are these words:
Unfortunately, the government and particularly the recruiting authorities failed to do just that. The Conservative government of Sir Robert Borden was severely handicapped throughout the war by the fact that its French-Canadian members represented a minority instead of a majority of their compatriots.
And the further quotation at page 90:
The year 1915 was marked not only by a magnificent expansion of Canada's wit effort, but also by the revival of racial conflict and a decided break in the unanimity of French- and English-speaking Canadians for the successful prosecution of the war. . . .
Underneath this seeming unanimity, there were forces, currents of emotion and counteremotion that were destined seriously .to impede Canada's war effort and practically to destroy the 1914 enthusiasm of French Canadians for active participation in the European war.
And on the following page:
It was most unfortunate for the cause of national solidarity that the controversy over the teaching of French in the Ontario schools should have come to a head at this moment to strengthen those forces of disunion. .	.	.
The agitation over the Ontario bilingual schools . . . results in growing bitterness between' the races until the average French Canadian lost a good deal of his enthusiasm for fighting England's battles.
And on page 92:
As a result of this instinctive feeling, it was not surprising to see French Canada's war effort become less enthusiastic as the Ontario schools controversy progressed.
And further clown on the same page:
The bitterness aroused by the dispute over the Ontario bilingual schools was responsible more than anything else for the gradual slowing up of the war effort of French Canada.
And at page 93:
To have such an issue raised at a moment when mutual tolerance and cooperation were essential to a successful prosecution of the war was unfortunate in the highest degree.
I realize the time at my disposal has practically elapsed. In conclusion I would ask every hon. member to take cognizance of this work, if he sincerely desires to be posted on the exact significance of conscription as a menace to the unity of the Canadian people.
May I terminate my observations by quoting from a letter received only a few days ago from a friend:
What aire we going to do about conscription, after the plebiscite? Why hold conscription like a red rag in front of a bull? Let ns bear in mind its true significance, and drop it like a curse. Let us direct all our efforts toward any other method of raising the manpower required for the outside defence of Canada. Let us eliminate from our vocabularies this element of national discord and cleavage, and get together on some common ground where susceptibilities are not smouldering at red heat. Let us act and talk more like brothers under the skin, which we really are. Let us consolidate our forces, not divide them, bearing in mind the tremendous task which we all have of winning this war at the side of our sister nations of the commonwealth.
To indicate that there are no hard feelings in my heart toward any hon. member who may have criticized me, and particularly toward the leader of the opposition, may I, through you, sir, and with my compliments, offer a gift of this book to the leader of the opposition so that he may have an opportunity of studying it and conveying some of its contents to his fellow members.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South):	Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention
to follow the arguments of the last speaker except to make reference to some of the statements which he made. He referred to the question of conscription. This question of conscription has been raised so often in this house that one would think we did not have conscription in Canada. We have conscription in Canada; let us face the fact. The only difference is that we have not conscription for overseas service. Boys are being taken away from the farms and factories of this country and conscripted into the Canadian army. I think we should make that perfectly clear and get away from this nonsense of intimating that we have not conscription in this country. Furthermore, I should have thought that the last speaker in his eloquent pleading for national unity would have committed himself as to where he stands on this question of the plebiscite and what active part he intends to
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Homuth

take to try to get the people of Canada to vote "yes" to relieve the government of restrictions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. gentleman that I have done so already.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I am glad to hear it, because the hon. member's speech this afternoon did anything but help to create unity in this country. I think the address of the hon. gentleman will do more to create disunity in Canada than any other thing.
I do not intend to deal with the general question of the plebiscite, because that has been dealt with already. The house has passed on the matter and we are going to have a plebiscite. I had thought that the discussion on the second reading of the bill was limited to a discussion of its principle. My own opinion is that the hon. member who has just spoken was entirely out of order. In fact, I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was out of order yesterday because there was very little discussion of the principle of the bill. What I want to deal with is the principle and the proponents of the bill.
I have listened carefully to the arguments which have been advanced for and against the plebiscite during the debate on the resolution and so far on the bill itself. I listened carefully to the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, which was practically all on the question of holding a plebiscite. This bill and those speeches must revive in the mind of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) some fond memories of his political career, and also of some of the speeches the Prime Minister has made in the past. I can imagine the Minister of Mines and Resources sitting in his seat and every once in a while giving a little squirm when some criticism of the War-time Elections Act and of Union government crossed the floor of the house, evidently aimed at the Conservative party but sometimes hitting him in passing. I can hear him saying, "Ouch, that hurts," when some of those barbs struck him. The Minister of Mines and Resources was first elected to the Canadian House of Commons under the War-time Elections Act, 1917, and his mind must have gone back to those days. I have here a few extracts from some of the speeches which the Minister of Mines and Resources made during that campaign. They are interesting when compared with his attitude to-day on this question and his very loyal-I think that is the best term to use-support which he gives the present Prime Minister.
Speaking at Carman, Manitoba, on December 3, 1917, the Minister of Mines and Resources, who was then a Union government candidate, said:
Conscript wealth as well as flesh and blood.

He offered hearty congratulations to the Liberals who because of their loyalty and sincerity had joined the Union government and deserted Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Then on December 13, 1917, he said:
Compulsory military service, as the Honourable Arthur Meighen has said, is the rock upon which Union government is built.
At that time he was a strong supporter of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. He followed his every speech and he watched his every gesture ; he considered him one of the great Canadians. He then went on to say:
There is no chance of a referendum if this Union government is defeated on Monday next. Canada will then be committed to a policy which will bring shame to her.
Sir Wilfrid had proposed a referendum. On December 14, 1917, there was a tremendous crowd in Grace church, Winnipeg. Speaking at that meeting the Minister of Mines and Resources said:
I do not question Sir Wilfrid Laurier's loyalty, but i do question the loyalty of those who are standing behind him in Quebec. The very best element in the Liberal party is in support of this Union government.
This Liberal party is now supported by all members, whether they come from other provinces or from the province of Quebec. Needless to say his leader, the present Prime Minister of Canada, was not in that group in 1917. The minister said:
When the boys go over the top there is no question as to whether they are Liberal or Conservative. Cannot we too stand united and go over the top on December 17?
The Prime Minister has talked a good deal about national unity. I should like to refer to a speech which he made in 1940 as it relates to-the bill now before the house. Referring to national unity, the Prime Minister said:
Least of all was it brought about by pledges to extend the life of parliament in a time of war without any reference to the people, or to form a so-called "national" government that might enforce conscription or disfranchise many classes of Canadian citizens. The memories of those experiences in the last war are still bitter in the minds of the Canadian people.
In dealing with the present bill, we can only do so perhaps by comparing it with the War-time Elections Act of 1917. The government has found that the country is at war and that it is necessary during this war to take a vote on a certain question. In arranging to take that vote they find that they have to present to the house a bill which will provide for those who may or may not be able to vote. They have a problem on their hands which to my mind they will find it difficult to solve. We must remember that in the county of Waterloo, in some of the neighbouring counties and in many other

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Homuth
places throughout Canada, whenever it has been found useful to use it since 1917, the old War-time Elections Act has been dragged out of the closet and waved before the eyes of electors to whom it might mean something. And so this bill is presented to the house. I think I am not unparliamentary, Mr. Speaker, when I say that this bill contains more political trickery than any other piece of legislation that has ever been introduced into the House of Commons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Is the hon. member supporting or opposing it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I shall tell my hon. friend all about that. But first I want to compare this bill with the Wartime Elections Act of 1917.	.
The act of 1917 contains clauses with which I thoroughly disagree, clauses which in my opinion were unfair and should never have been embodied in an election act. But this bill contains clauses which are or might be just as vicious. By the act of 1917 the franchise was extended to certain classes of women in this country. There was no women's franchise in Canada in 1917. The first time the franchise was extended to women was in Ontario in the elections of 1919. But in the act of 1917 the franchise was given to the wives and mothers of men who were overseas, and after all, I know of no one who was more interested in the war than the wives and mothers who were waiting patiently and anxiously for husband or son to come home, waiting perhaps only to receive a telegram saying they would never be home again.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman is not suggesting that they are disfranchised under this bill?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I am not suggesting that at all. I am comparing some of the clauses of the act of 1917 with some of the terms of this bill, which certainly are not clear to me, and unless they are very much modified, will not be clear to the electors.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) the other day referred to paragraph (c) of subsection 2 of section 4 of this bill, which deals with those who are barred from voting on the plebiscite through being barred in the province in which they live. He made an eloquent plea that the great Liberal party should never do a thing like this; he appealed to the great principles of Liberalism in urging that this provision should be struck out of the bill. So far as pleading for the principles of Liberalism is concerned, he was pleading for something that is deader than a mackerel. Nevertheless he made the statement, and I reiterate it, that this clause is one of the most dangerous that could be put in any
election act. Suppose a German warship should be able to approach, let us say, some town in Prince Edward Island, and it was feared that German fifth columnists in Prince Edward Island might become active, and that therefore the legislature immediately met and decided to intern many of them and deprive them of their right to vote in a provincial election. That would mean that everyone of German origin throughout Canada would be debarred1 from voting on the plebiscite, and that might happen two days before the plebiscite vote was taken. People of German origin throughout Canada would be debarred from voting on the plebiscite, thousands of mothers and fathers whose sons went overseas in the last war and died for this country- families who have been settled here for a hundred: and twenty to a hundred and fifty years and have played their part in every war in which Canada and the empire have been engaged. That disqualification might apply to other races. Why the clause is in there at all I do not know unless the government was given to understand that it applies to the Japanese because of the situation in British Columbia. If that be so, let us be frank and put it in the bill that the Japanese are barred from voting. But why should the bill contain such a general clause as this?
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) made a point yesterday which I think was well taken-that this bill would bring about a complete change in our constitutional set-up and system of government in Canada. He made that so clear that the point needs no labouring. But I go further. I remember what happened when the National Resources Mobilization Act was before the house, and the national registration. We had a meeting in the railway committee room at which Mr. Justice Davis and the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who was then also Minister of National War Services, discussed this whole matter with the members of this house. At that time they said there would be no exemptions whatsoever under the National Resources Mobilization Act. They did provide, however, for indefinite postponements for members of two religious creeds, the Doukhobors and the Mennonites. But for fear there would be resentment among the other peoples of this country because the Doukhobors and the Mennonites were being granted an indefinite postponement the government decided to establish and did establish work camps, and the boys of those- two faiths were taken from their homes, from the farms of this country, and sent into those camps to build useless roads that some tourists may drive over years hence. But in western Canada the Doukhobors, I understand, refused to
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Homuth

go into these camps, and so they were taken before the courts and sentenced, some of them to serve time in gaol, some to pay a fine; and in the event of not paying the fine they had to serve an extra month in gaol. Now they are free. I doubt whether the government will call them and fine them and gaol them again, 'because they have purchased their freedom by serving two months in gaol and paying a fine of $200, or serving three months in gaol. From a casual reading of this bill one would think that these people were denied the right to vote on the plebiscite, or that if they did vote on it they would be subject to military service. That is the general impression one gets from a first reading of the bill. But as a matter of fact it does not deny to them the right to vote on the plebiscite. The conscientious objectors, the Mennonites and the Douklhabors, can vote on this plebiscite, and that is part of the trickery that is in this bill. The government should make it abundantly clear to the people of this country whether or not these people are going to be allowed to vote on the plebiscite. It is not clear- now.
Take the case of a Mennonite or a Douk-hobor family, consisting of the father, the mother, three daughters over twenty-one and therefore old enough to vote, and a son of military age. If the son votes he is liable to military service, but the father, the mother and the three daughters can vote, knowing that they will not be required to serve; the son refrains from voting and is not liable to military service; and there are five votes in that family against the plebiscite. That is according to a provision of this bill. The government is in the position of saying that while on the face of it it looks as though these people dare not vote, in a very subtle way we have arranged that they can vote, because the only one who is debarred from voting is the son of military age. These people do not have to fight for their country or serve in any capacity, and five out of a family of six will be permitted to vote against the plebiscite. Surely that is not the type of legislation we want. .

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: What does the hon. member suggest?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
What do I suggest? I suggest that the government come out honestly and say where they stand on this matter, whether these people have or have not the right to vote. So far as I am concerned, let me tell my hon. friend that any citizens of this country who, while enjoying the freedom, the opportunities and the protection which this country and this empire give them, are not prepared to serve in the military forces or the non-combatant forces

to the very limits of which they are capable, are not fit to be called Canadians. That is my opinion, and I have no hesitation in expressing it. The Mennonites are not averse to serving; they are prepared to do anything they can in support of our war effort so long as they do not have to bear arms and kill, because to do so is against the principles of their religion. But there are many things which they could do, and do much better than they are being done to-day, without dragging them off their farms and putting them in camps.
Let me say further that this bill does not jibe with the war service act, because, while these provisions are in the bill, these people are subject to being taken out and put in those camps. I wonder whether the Secretary of State drew up this bill. I do not know, but I should not be surprised if he did, because it is just about as double-barrelled as many of the orders in council which came from the Labour department when he was in charge of it, and the meaning of which half the time we did not know.
Also, Mr. Speaker, there is no provision to get out the vote. The Prime Minister called yesterday for national unity; he asked hon. members to go home, organize their ridings, engage the help of service clubs and other people to serve as returning officers, scrutineers, and so forth, for no compensation. I believe many people can be persuaded to da it. But when he calls for national unity, the place for him to start, so far as this plebiscite is concerned, is within the ranks of his own party; because the only people in this house who have said that they would refuse to release the government from its promise to-the people are members within his own ranks, and the only organizations in respect of this plebiscite in Canada to-day are those which are opposed to it. To judge by some of the speeches delivered in this chamber, and by a meeting which was held in Montreal and ended in a riot, a tremendous organization is going on against releasing the government from its promise. Now, what does the government intend to do in order to ensure that there is an equally strong, strenuous and active organization to see that there is a sufficient vote to release it from its promise? It has a tremendous responsibility. I am fearful of the position of this country in the eyes not only of our own people but of the other-nations of the world, if this plebiscite should be adverse to releasing the government. It would be a tragedy were such a thing ta occur.

Well, then, why not
support it?

Now, Mr. Speaker, I say this, and in all seriousness. The Prime Minister has a tremendous job on his hands. He has first of all to close up his own ranks, to see to it that his own supporters in this house get out and do the job which he is asking us to do. He need have no fears about what we are going to do. He need have no doubt about the stand which the opposition will take. Our leader has made it abundantly plain. But if this plebiscite results in a negative vote, Canada will stand in a very serious position.
This w:eek we had a secret session of the house to get information on our war effort. In May we are going to take a plebiscite; the people are to be asked to relieve the government of a promise. Yet they have no such knowledge as we have of the war situation. It is time that the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet told them plainly just what that situation is, and how great a danger it holds for Canada and for everything we hold dear. Rather than see the plebiscite defeated I would endorse action by the government to withdraw the whole thing from this house and forget the matter entirely. Unfortunately the government, in its effort not to promote national unity but to play with this question, has grabbed a wild cat by the tail.

The hon. gentleman who just sat down stated that the government has a wild cat by the tail and cannot let go. Possibly the illustration is unfortunate from his point of view, because hon. gentlemen opposite did have that wild cat by the tail and have now let go.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). It is notable for what
it does not say rather than for what it says. The argument against the plebiscite was riding high, wide and handsome until a few days ago, when the opposition observed that they had a wild cat by the tail. I note that to-day they no longer oppose the plebiscite-it is too much like a wild cat to hold by the tail'; they limit themselves to making attacks on small details of the bill which no doubt will be settled in committee in a way satisfactory to all concerned.
For instance there was the attack by the hon. gentleman from Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) on section 5 of the bill, which is directed possibly towards the Mennonite or Doukhobor vote of the west. That section provides that those who vote on the plebiscite may not later claim exemption from military service. The hon. gentleman worked himself up into a great heat and fury about some Mennonite family who might all vote with the exception only of those liable for military service. I asked him what he suggested and he went into a heated reply but did not answer the question. A friend at my side handed me a book in which he pointed to a quotation from some philosopher of old who said "in politics heat is in inverse proportion to knowledge". I thought it applicable and timely because, although the hon. gentleman got very warm, he did not give me any knowledge as to what he proposed to do. What would hon. members do under these circumstances, granted the picture is correct as he has presented it? Would they disfranchise all the Mennonites and all the Doukhobors? Would they not make those who vote liable to military service? It seems to me that a practical viewpoint rather than a condition of heat is required when one is discussing the details of a bill. Is not the bill as it stands probably the best solution that could be obtained under the circumstances? It provides that young men capable of military service may not vote on the question and later claim exemption. .
I am inclined to compliment the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) upon his attack on section 3 of the bill. There are before the house at the moment two principles involved in this bill. One is the principle of giving to the executive the power to have general plebiscites on any question and at all times. That is what is expressed in the bill. But we now have the intimation by the government that this will later be changed in committee. W'ere the bill to stand as it now reads, I would approach it with a great deal of doubt; I do not like these general powers given to an executive unless there is a distinct understanding as to how they are to be used.

speechtext:
Yes; I thank my hon.
friend for the correction. When that measure was revived-I do not remember that there was a vote in the house, but, at that time, I suppose no hon. member, whether in the executive or out of it, anticipated that by this time there would be some twenty thousand orders in council passed. I suppose there was no one who anticipated that these orders in council would go into such broad measures as the limitation of prices, the regulation of wages and other such matters of a civil nature. When you hand over power to an executive you must look to it that the limitations are such that the executive will not go further than you would yourself. I have looked with regret on the limitation of the activities of parliament and the absorption of so much power by the executive, so I would hesitate to give to the executive the power to hold general plebiscites on any question. I compliment the hon. member for Lake Centre for having objected while this only was before us. But with the assurance that we now have from the government I think we may assume that what is before us is a plebiscite on the question:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
That is the matter before us now.
I did not speak in the debate on the address in reply. It was very largely given up to the discussion of the pros and cons of conscription. I did not speak because I felt that practically every veiwpoint was covered and because I felt that very little was to be gained by much talking on that most contentious problem; that the more one spoke on it, the more angry one became, the further the disputants drew apart, and the more difficult became the situation presented to the Canadian people. There would

be very little difficulty indeed, were hon. members on this side of the house left free from the influence of stirred-up public opinion abroad, in arranging some reasonable solution of that question. The whole difficulty arises from much talk and perhaps a too partisan attitude on the question.
I did not take part in the argument. Yet I feel that for the sake of my own con*-stituents I should not allow this opportunity to go by to put on record where I stand on this question.
I am neither a conscriptionist nor an anti-conscriptionist. There are two main arguments on the matter. There is first the desire which I and many others have for a voluntary army rather than a conscript army, because we believe that the volunteer army is better. I can go back in my own memory to the time: when we used to hold almost in contempt the conscript armies of Europe, and used to look with pride on the British armies of those days which were raised by voluntary enlistment. I am reinforced in my opinion by the remarks of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), who said it was most important that our present splendid volunteer army be reinforced 'by volunteers and not by conscripts. I am satisfied that one of the prime requisites-or perhaps that is a little too strongly stated; that one of the best qualifications for joining the armed forces of Canada is willingness to serve. It is a most important factor; and I cannot see, as some people argue, that anything is to be gained, as far as the army is concerned, by abolishing voluntary service and replacing it with some kind of compulsion. So I am not in favour of compulsion for compulsion's sake.
On the other hand, I have before me a comment made by Mr. Winston Churchill in one of his speeches, published in his recent book, which I should like to read to the house. He was speaking about the conscription act that was introduced into the British house during this war, and said:
At the beginning of the war of 1914 we soon had a million volunteers on our hands, for the bulk of whom no weapons were available. Ultimately over two million men demanded to be led to the front. But after that the limits of voluntary recruitment were exhausted. The war continued and the armies could not be maintained. Then we had the hateful spectacle of volunteers who had been wounded twice or even thrice being sent back to the trenches, and of regular soldiers who had served two whole years in the front line being deprived of their right to claim expiry of their eomitriact: This proved intolerable to the national sense of justice. Moreover, two million households and families whose menfolk had borne the whole burden were infuriated by the fact that, there were very large numbers of perfectly fit men remaining at home, filling at higher wages

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Roebuck
the jobs of those who had volunteered. It was this sense of wrong and injustice, which spread through the country in the spring and summer of 1916, that alone carried the conscription bill.
So you 'have these two conflicting ideas: the value of a volunteer army on the one hand, and the utter unfairness of voluntary service on the other; the unfairness of having in the army only those whose public spirit is sufficiently great to induce them to enlist, and the unfairness of allowing those whose public spirit is insufficient to remain in the safety and comfort of their homes. Those two arguments are irreconcilable; the longer you talk about them, the more they clash. So you come to the point where you must make practical decisions, rather than an out-and-out* choice between the two.
The time has not yet arrived in Canada, as it did in Great Britain, when people are outraged at the unfairness of the situation. If the war continues; if casualties increase; if there are published in the press long lists of names of those who have been lost; if many months of arduous service go by, that feeling will become overwhelming in this country, the unfairness of keeping the public-spirited men in the front lines while the loafers, the shirkers, sit comfortably at home. Therefore the desire for the fairness of selective service will overcome our desire for a volunteer army. We must put ourselves in a position to do what is right under the circumstances as they exist from time to time.
For that reason I am heartily in accord with the bill now before the house. The opposition to it is perhaps uninformed; perhaps it refuses actually to see or consider the points involved. May I lay before the house a resolution which I recently received from the clerk of the city council of Toronto. Mr. J. W. Somers, city clerk, wrote me as follows:
Pursuant to instruction, I forward herewith, a copy of a resolution which was adopted by the city council, at its meeting on February 9, 1942, as follows:
"Whereas, it is the proposed intention of the federal government to hold a plebiscite on the general question of conscription and whereas the cost of the same has been estimated to be well over one million dollars, and whereas, at this time, leadership is needed to be given, more than ever, by the elected government at Ottawa, and whereas the holding of such a plebiscite will tend to harm rather than help Canada's war effort;
"Be it resolved: that this city council petitions the federal government to reconsider its decision on a plebiscite of this nature being placed before the peoples of this country at this most critical time, and further, a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Prime Minister of Canada and his cabinet and to all federal representatives of this city."
I received that resolution, and it may be of some interest if I may be permitted to read my reply. I wrote the city clerk in part as follows:
I am glad to know the view of the city council in respect to this matter, and thank you for your letter.
It strikes me, however, that the resolution is incomplete, and I would like a little more information. I am of opinion that our selective service law requires amendment, and I think the council agrees with me on this. It does not make clear, however, how the government is to free itself of the pledge given to the public, if a plebiscite is not held. I am sure that the council does not suggest that the government violate or disregard its pledge, and I am also fairly confident that it does not advocate that the government carry on indefinitely as we are. As the act now stands, we could not send draftees across the international border into the United States, nor could we, for instance, hold the Aleutian islands against the Japanese with drafted men.
I value the thought and wisdom of the city council and I would like to know what it is they actually propose.
That letter was dated February 16, and so far I have not received a reply. In private discussions of the matter I have found that when you bring somebody right up against the question: "Do you advocate that we stay as we are, or do you advocate that the government violate a pledge?" you seldom obtain an answer, certainly not from a partisan.
I think many people have not really realized what the attack on the plebicsite means.
Yesterday the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) advised that all 245 members of this house join together and adopt a resolution releasing ourselves from the pledge. The hon. member seemed to think we might then in honour proceed to deal with the matter as we saw fit.
I spoke in the city of Toronto on Sunday evening on this question, to a very considerable audience. I told them that I personally, in that very hall, and from that very platform had told those very people that if the government was returned to power, the government led by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) they would not have conscription. I was justified in that statement because I had the pledge of the Prime Minister, and I also pointed out in that speech that I also had the pledge of the then leader of the opposition, Doctor Manion. Therefore, no matter which party won, there would not be conscription in Canada during this war, until another general election took place.
I told these people that I personally did not stand for broken pledges and that I would not be a party to making the breaking of pledges a principle of political action. That
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Roebuck

is my view, and that is where I hold myself right now. I will not take part in the breaking of these pledges; and, Mr. Speaker, I do not see how, if I joined with the hon. member for New Westminster, (Mr. Reid), and the two of us concocted something, I would in any way relieve myself from the pledge. Nor if I added all the gentlemen around me would I relieve myself from it. Nor indeed would I help myself in any way if I joined with the hon. member for Yale and the leader of the opposition.
There is an old story to the effect that when thieves fall out, honest men get their due. It is when thieves join together that honest men must beware. One cannot recover from a pledge solemnly given to the public by joining in some kind of conspiracy to get our own way without their consent. We would not increase by one iota the morality of our action by each severally violating his pledge, in association with all other members of parliament who were violating theirs.
Therefore in my judgment, so far as I can see, there is no way of handling the practical needs of the situation other than by taking a plebiscite and asking for a release. That is the honest way, the decent way; it is needed; it is necessary.
The hon. member for Waterloo South was most anxious about the vote, whether it was or was not going to carry. He complained that we should throw obligation on hon. members of the oposition to have it carried. His question was: What is the government going to do? Well, I throw back the question. I can tell him what I will do, because I have already done it. I advocate voting "yes" on the plebiscite. What are you going to do? There is no doubt about what the great majority, at least 95 per cent, of hon. members on this side of the house will do. Now, what will the opposition do?
There is no lack of money, no lack of organization on the Conservative side. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) referred to the junta which recently met in Toronto to stimulate an all-out war effort, a junta which spent thousands of dollars upon advertising in the public press.

I want my riding to understand that I am going to vote "yes" for this bill, that I am going to urge them to vote "yes" on the plebiscite.
There are two phases to this question. One phase has been dealt with so thoroughly by the Prime Minister that there is practically nothing left to be said on the question. His magnificent speech yesterday was conclusive, but one thing sticks in my mind.
We have been dealing with the question of how we can raise men, whether by voluntary enlistment or by conscription. There is, however, a second phase which has not been mentioned but which is just about as important. It occurs after these men have been raised; and a considerable number have been raised by the selective system. As I stated in my letter to the city council of Toronto, we are not in a position to use these men if it is necessary to cross the international border between ourselves and the United States, or in order to protect the islands on the Pacific coast. It is most unlikely, but it might happen that an enemy expeditionary force be landed on the Pacific coast and that it hold the passes of the Rockies against us. Our only hope of dislodging such a force would be by sending men to the south and bringing them up along the coast. As things stand now, we could not do that. We cannot raise men for service overseas by selective call. And having so raised men, we cannot use them on any expedition which takes them across our borders or beyond the three-mile limit.
So I submit that, whether you are a con-scriptionist or an anti-conscriptionist, the necessity for the correction of this situation is such that you should vote "yes" on the plebiscite.
