speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to follow the previous speaker, but I was interested in the reference he made to the two cities in the good city of Toronto. That is a situation which applies and has applied everywhere for many years. Lord Beaconsfield, at one time Prime Minister of Great Britain, wrote a book about the two nations, the two Englands. He wrote about the England1 of the rich, the wealthy and the aristocrats, and the England of the toiling masses, the mud sills upon which the other England rested. He made a very good job of it too.
There are one or two- points in connection with this bill upon which I should like to comment. One has been cleared up to some extent by the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) yesterday. It is to be regretted that his speech of yesterday was not made during the debate on the address. It

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Maclnnis

would appear that he was speaking then with the by-elections in mind, while his speech yesterday quite properly had the plebiscite in mind. As the discussion went on during the debate on the address I was at a loss to know whether the proposed plebiscite was being introduced because the cabinet felt that it was desirable to have this additional power or because of the slings and arrows of the "committee of two hundred". The speeches of hon. members opposite throughout the address debate stressed two things, criticism of the "committee of two hundred" and satisfaction with the voluntary system. This was true to such an extent that I felt somewhat concerned about the fate of the plebiscite.
If we are going to have a plebiscite-and evidently we are-it is absolutely necessary that it should carry. Neither the government nor the country can afford to have the plebiscite defeated, or carried without strong support. It seems to me that the government will be in a bad position, both for its own sake and for the sake of the country's war effort if the vote is indecisive, that is, if there is only a small majority in favour of the plebiscite, or if there is a majority in favour of it in one part of the country and against it in another, even though there be an over-all majority. I am going to indicate to the government where the danger of the plebiscite being defeated1 lies, if it is going to be submitted as it now reads.
In both the speech from the throne and the speech by the deputy governor general upon the prorogation of parliament there is given in unmistakable language the reasons which the government should put forward as to why the plebiscite must carry. Speaking at the prorogation of parliament on January 21 last, the deputy governor general said:
Since the present session opened, we have witnessed 'the extension of war until, to-day, it encompasses the globe. A.s aggression has succeeded aggression, the active resistance of free peoples everywhere has risen to meet it. The myth of national isolation has vanished from the earth. It is now recognized that the freedom of each nation is bound up in the freedom of all.
I agree with that, but what has been said by hon. members opposite since parliament opened on January 22 to bring home to the people of Canada, to bring home to the isolationists of Canada, that Canada's cause is one with the cause of every free nation in the world? A similar statement is made in the speech from the throne. The very first paragraph reads:
There no longer can be a.ny question as to the character and scope of the present war. ft is a world-wide conflict between irreconcilable farces. On every continent, including the confines of our own, and on all oceans, forces that
[Mr. Maclnnis.3
aim at world domination oppose forces that seek the preservation of freedom. In every quarter of the globe, civilization is confronted by savagery.
It appears to me that in that paragraph lies the reason why the government of Canada should have power to use the whole resources of Canada in men and materials to fight the enemy wherever the enemy may be found.
As I said, the speech of the Prime Minister yesterday to some extent cleared away one of my fears, that is, that the government did not sufficiently realize the urgency of the situation. It is urgent. Speaking for myself and also, I think, for the group with whom I sit, we believe the government should be given the freedom and authority which it seeks. But we are not satisfied to leave the matter there. From what I hear from my own province of British Columbia, I am satisfied that if the plebiscite is put in its present form to the people of Canada without some assurance that not only men will be conscripted but also the wealth and industry and material resources of this country to the last ounce and last cent and that those resources are going to be used, the plebiscite will be defeated in British Columbia just as sure as the people are asked to vote on it. The same thing will happen, I believe, in other provinces.
The Prime Minister in his speech yesterday said that the plebiscite was not a question of conscription but a question of freeing the government's hands. It is just nonsense to talk in that way because, when the people of my province are voting on the plebiscite, they are not voting to free the hands of the government. No they are voting on conscription. When the people in the province of Quebec vote on the plebiscite, what are they voting on? They are voting on the question of conscription. No mere play with words can alter that fact. The plebiscite says that it is for the purpose of freeing the government's hands, but the government's hands are tied only in one respect, in respect only of the compulsory enlistment of men for overseas service. Let the government be frank with the people. Let the government take the people into its confidence. Let the government appeal to the intelligence of the people and tell them exactly what the circumstances are and what they are voting for. Let the government demonstrate itself by its dealings with the people that it believes in those phrases it uses when it says we are fighting for freedom and democracy and such things as that.
It is essential that the government should have this power. But that does not necessarily mean that Canada would send more men out of the country than it is sending now. That would depend a great deal on how the war goes. To

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Maclnnis
be quite frank, I am not sure that anything has been gained so far in a military way because of the men Canada sent out of the country. I am saying that nothing has been gained up until the present time, and that the men could have been used to much better advantage at home. But I say again that this does not mean that I am opposed to sending them out of the country if that is considered necessary. They should be sent where and when they are needed. We are fighting a worldwide war. We are fighting out in the far east. Why in the world should Canada send soldiers to the far east to fight the Japanese when China has her millions who are anxious to fight the Japanese. Not only that, but her soldiers are acclimatized and know and understand the country where the fighting is taking place. Canada's work in these circumstances would be to supply the Chinese with the arms with which to fight. We cannot do both things. We cannot be on the sea and on the fighting front in the far east, and at the same time be producing equipment in the factories in Canada.
Since it is nearly six o'clock I dhall try to conclude before the house rises. In my opinion there are two things the government should do if it wants to get a satisfactory affirmative vote on the plebiscite. First, it should give a solemn undertaking, just as binding as the pledges that were given in regard to enlistment for service overseas, that concurrently with the conscription of man-power there shall be conscription of industry and finance. I want to say here as clearly and as definitely as I can that if that is not done, there is great danger that the plebiscite will be defeated. Second, as I have already said, the government should tell the people the urgency of the war situation and indicate clearly to them that it is going, if necessary, to use the power it is asking for-going to use the whole resources of the country. I ask the government to observe the changes that are taking place in the mind of the people all over the world. There is a change of mind in Great Britain. Many people are convinced that our reverses in the far east have been to a large extent due to our refusal in the past to grant or guarantee to the people of the far east equality of status with ourselves. If we do not do that-and there is rising hope that it will be done-we are not going to get as much out of this war as we thought we would.
There are one or two suggestions I should like to make in regard to the taking of the vote. There is danger, unless a great deal of enthusiasm is created in connection with the plebiscite, that the vote will be very small. We know that in parliamentary elections great pressure has to be used1 to get the people out 44561-S5i
to the polls. The opposing candidates have an incentive to apply that pressure, and they try to get out every possible vote. But such an incentive will be largely lacking in taking the vote on the plebiscite. There may be a general desire to get out a large vote, but there will be no specific desire unless the thing is well organized. We should see that every possible vote is polled. I understand that the statement has been made by the chief electoral officer that the enumeration of voters and the other work necessary for the taking of the vote will be carried out on a patronage basis. It is a terrible thing that the government should allow a statement like that to be made.

I desire to occupy a very brief

When the speech from the throne was brought down on January 22 and it was announced that the ministry would seek release from its pre-election pledge in regard to the man-power situation by means of a plebiscite, there was not the slightest intimation that the bill to be brought down would be anything other than an enabling measure designed to fulfil the promise contained in the speech from the throne and providing a way and means whereby the people would be asked to say whether they released the Prime Minister (Mr, Mackenzie King) and the government from a past commitment with respect to a particular pledge.
When I made my remarks on January 26 they were predicated on the theory that there would be brought down an enabling measure of a particular kind and nature, patterned in some degree at least upon the Plebiscite Act of 1898, designed to enable the government to secure release from a particular commitment. When the Prime Minister made his speech on the same day the whole underlying reasoning of his statement with regard to the legislation for the plebiscite was based on the same theory. Again in the speech which I made on Wednesday the ,18th instant, just prior to the vote, I predicated my remarks

on that same theory. Again in the remarks which I made on the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill on Monday last I based my entire argument on the assumption that the bill was to deal with a particular situation in a particular way. And when on the same day the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) made his speech supporting the resolution it was, as I interpreted it, predicated on the same theory, that the house was being asked to pass a measure designed to meet a particular situation which had arisen, and from which the government sought release, and on that theory alone and to meet that situation alone. If the hon. Secretary of State had any other design, I should say that he most skilfully concealed it.
When I spoke on that resolution on Monday last I had not seen the 'bill. I had tried to get a copy-

That is
another matter. The Secretary of State made it clear that the specific question would not be in the bill. I tried again early on Tuesday last and again was denied it for the same reason. I am not complaining of any lack of courtesy; the bill had not been printed. I did not apply to the minister personally for a copy of the bill; perhaps I might have done so and probably he would have given me at least a draft of it. But it was not until late on Tuesday that the bill was distributed.
I then discovered really for the first time that the bill as introduced and given first reading was not designed particularly to carry out the announcement in the speech from the throne and the announcement in the Prime Minister's speech of January 26. But to my surprise it was and is general in its nature and is designed to be general, and to import into the constitution of Canada an entirely new principle. This is a general act to be introduced in the statutes of this country, to be there for all time unless it is changed. I am going to speak later about the promise, the very definite promise, which the Prime Minister made this afternoon.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
To me that was a rather startling situation, the importation into the constitutional practice of this country of a new constitutional principle, a new instrument in government. It is chiefly because of that that I am participating even briefly in this debate to-night.
This is not only an innovation in our constitution; but, may I say, it is a violation of the political principles on which the Canadian constitution is established, principles which have been developed over the centuries by the matured experience of British statesmen; and I certainly object to the introduction of a new constitutional principle in the system of our government in Canada.

speechtext:
I am coming to that. But this protest is on a matter of principle and I am entitled to put it on the record. I shall deal with the altered situation in due course, and if any credit is coming to the government and the Prime Minister I am quite prepared to give it to them. But I do protest against the introduction of this new departure in constitutional practice. This is not the bill we were promised.
There is one other protest I want to make. This bill, even if altered-and I am going to deal with that in a few minutes-merely sets up the substantive proposals of the government. It leaves the rest to a large number of regulations which we have not seen, but which I understand are ready to be taken to the committee with the bill-regulations which are in themselves legislative in character.
Let me call attention to the elections act. We have in Canada an elections act, containing a very large number of sections; and all the legislative features relating to the carrying on of elections in this country are incorporated in that legislation itself. Accompanying that election law are an equally large or perhaps a larger number of regulations. but those regulations are in no sense legislative; they are explanatory, instructional, interpretative.
Let me make that point clear. Here it is proposed to do by regulation something that under the election law of this country we do by legislation. That itself is a departure from established principles. Of course I have not seen the regulations; none of us have. We do not know what they contain; but I would not be astonished if a large number of
sections of the regulations deal with this question of legislating in respect of the plebiscite that is to be held. That, I think, is quite improper. That function should be reserved to parliament.
Let me turn now to the bill itself. As I said before, it merely sets up the substantive law relating to the holding of a plebiscite; and, as I stated a while ago, until it is changed^ it provides for the taking of a plebiscite on any question that may be submitted by authority of the governor in council, under proclamation. The Prime Minister stated very early in the discussion, I think, that the question would be incorporated in the bill itself, and for that I thank him; but I am going to ask him to go further than that. Unless there would be a violation of some understanding, arrangement or agreement, I suggest to him that this bill should be entirely revamped, so that we shall not even have the appearance of incorporating into the constitutional system of this country the principle of the plebiscite. That I think he should do; and I think he has almost gone that far. Not only should he limit the operation of the statute that will be passed to the holding of this one particular plebiscite; the whole bill should be redrafted on that theory and along the line of the bill that was passed at the time the temperance plebiscite was taken away back in the last century. I believe the proper way to do that would be to withdraw this bill and bring in a new bill, based upon that theory. I do not know whether the government will do that, but I offer the suggestion. I do not think it would delay matters; so far as I am concerned I would undertake that there would be no delay, though of course one would want to see the bill.
If the government will not yield to that suggestion, then, in accordance with the undertaking given explicitly this afternoon, I ask them to give instructions to the committee, of which they will be in complete control, that the bill be revamped in committee along the lines I have suggested. I submit with great seriousness that there is a principle at stake, that this is a violation of the principle of responsible government as we understand it in Canada. If we once incorporate a principle like this into the constitutional practice of Canada,we shall have departed from every principle of representative and parliamentary government that we have followed down through the decades since Canada has been a confederation, and for decades before that under the British constitution. Under our practice the people of the country delegate to their elected representatives power to make
87o	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
laws in accordance with the constitution of the country. The principle of the plebiscite is the negation of responsible government, and so is the referendum. I did not quite understand the reference made by the Prime Minister yesterday to the referendum. I have never heard anyone recommend a referendum; at least I have not done so. I have not mentioned the question of a referendum, which of course stands upon a somewhat different principle. A plebiscite may or may not be binding upon the government that submits it, but a referendum has to do with a particular statute or proposal, and when submitted to the people it becomes binding upon the government. As I understand1 it, that, in a word, is the distinction between the two. I could not quite appreciate the point of the questions which the Prime Minister directed at me and others across the gangway here. We have never advocated a referendum. We are opposed to both referendum and plebiscite, but since the Prime Minister is bound to have a plebiscite I say, let him have it; let us get it over with; let us limit it to the particular situation and that alone, and let us not hear any more about it as an integral part of the system of responsible government in a British legislature.

He asked that the public give the government a free hand. For different reasons we want the government to have a free hand. He pointed out the distinction between the legal power possessed at this time by the government, and the moral authority which it possesses, or should possess.
With respect to the legal aspect of the matter, there is not any doubt about it that parliament is sovereign and supreme. I have heard the Prime Minister ring the changes of that phrase on many, many occasions in the house. Parliament has full legal power to pass any legislation. But he bases this on a high moral plane. He says that the one limitation is a moral obligation he owes the people, and he devoted a great deal of his speech to that issue.
He made a case-of course we can have our own opinions as to whether it was a good or a bad one. But he certainly made a case at least to the satisfaction of his followers. Now I put this to him: Is the moral obligation he described of such a nature as to prevent the government from doing what is necessary in wartime, with an invasion threatened, and if the necessities of the situation are as many people believe them to be, or believe that they may become? If the Prime Minister held the opinion that it was necessary to change the mobilization act by eliminating the limiting clause, would he pause to take a plebiscite? Would he do that, at a time when the country was in danger?
Of course he denies the truth of the premise. His suggestion is that the situation is not that bad now, that we are doing nicely. Yet the war comes home to us nearer, nearer and
nearer every day. We grant-he grants-I grant-we all grant that parliament has legal power. He says the one defect is the moral obligation. Is that a detriment to doing what we ought to do, if it is the right thing to do? What did the people send us here for? Why did they give my right hon. friend such an overwhelming mandate on March 26, 1940? It was to carry on the war to a successful conclusion, no matter what the cost, no matter what the needs might be. There was no limitation from the people, because conscription as I understand it was not an issue; certainly it was not an issue with me.

I say the Prime Minister, when he talks about moral obligations-and especially in the light of the admission he has now made-was putting up a straw man to knock down again. He has proved it himself by his utterances here to-night.
In days gone by the Prime Minister and his government have not always been so concerned about political morality. When I heard him speak yesterday I could not help recalling the days of Beauharnois. I remember the political morality of Beauharnois- how the Beauharnois corporation had applied to his government for the passage of an order in council allowing the deflection of a certain number of cubic feet per second of water through their canal at Beauharnois. I remember how the application was held off, and off, and off until the stage had been fully set. Then the government passed an order in council authorizing the diversion. We all know what happened. Hundreds of thousands of dollars contributed by the public of Canada to Beauharnois securities, I shall not say were stolen by the promoters, but were taken from those funds put up by the public and passed along by the promoters to the organizers of the Liberal party.

I wonder why my hon. friend would make a statement of that kind? He knows as well as I with respect to Beauharnois that not only was no charge of any kind whatsoever proved against the government, but the government's record in the matter was as straight as anything could possibly be. In addition to that, while hon. members like himself tried to make a case against the government before the public in one, two or three general elections, on every such occasion the public sent back this government with a stronger majority than ever.
My hon. friend had better be careful what he says when he talks about moral obligations. Something can be said from this side of the house, if he begins to reflect upon anyone here.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I am not reflecting upon the government; I am reflecting upon the Liberal party. I never heard it said that it was actionable to libel a party. If it were, there would be a good many libel actions in this country. My only answer is to ask hon. gentlemen to recall the speech which the Prime Minister made from this side of the chamber in regard to the Beauharnois transaction.
Another thing about pledges. I recall the platform of 1919; I recall the various planks in that platform. Among others was one with respect to the British preference. Does the Prime Minister say that those pledges in the 1919 platform were kept? I remember hearing something about their being just a chart to go by. In his opening speech in the 1940 election the Prime Minister said that there would be extravagant statements made and promises given. Those are not his exact words. That is always done during the course of an election by everyone in the hope of influencing the votes of the electors. I do not think these extreme appeals meet with great success very often. I have been most careful about making concrete pledges because I have always had a horror of not being able to keep any concrete promise which I made. I am leery about making election pledges. I do not think promises of public works and the expenditure of the taxpayers' money and that sort of thing ever brought many votes. I know that actual expenditures on public works prior to an election do not bring votes; all they do is to make enemies. These simply illustrate the futility of using the taxpayers' funds in an attempt to influence votes. Other people's experience may be different, but that is mine.
The Prime Minister made a strong political speech. I thought he was rather truculent in dealing with the political aspects of the question he was debating. Mr. Speaker, during the long weeks of debate in which we have indulged it has been difficult at times to be sure just what are the questions at issue, and there has been so much of almost irrelevant talk and so much of what appears to be a failure to see what are the relevant issues that the whole matter has been somewhat confusing.
It seems to me that there are three main matters which probably it would be fitting for me to touch upon in the short time at my disposal. The first is the question of a plebiscite. I am not sure that I entirely concur in the views of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) with respect to plebiscites. As a matter of fact the plebiscite is a device which is only being tried. It has been experimented with considerably in various parts of the world, but I am not sure that what we know concerning the success or failure of attempts in other lands is sufficiently definite to justify us in drawing any very clear conclusions. But this I think all of us desiring to preserve democracy must grant, that democracy is passing through testing fires. Times are changed; events happen fast; news travels speedily, and opinions change rapidly. Any government, particularly in a democracy, should keep in contact with the will of the governed, for governments must govern in accordance with the will of the governed. How any government in such hectic times as these can keep in contact with the will of the governed over a period1 of four full years without recourse to some such device as a plebiscite, no member of the

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Blackmore
opposition has succeeded in making clear to me. It would seem, therefore, that perhaps the plebiscite might be tried. We may find in it an instrument which will assist us greatly in carrying on a democracy.
There are, however, certain conditions which we must take care to see applied. In the first place, I would say that the subject of a plebiscite needs to be rather simple. The wording of the question submitted must also be very clear, and the question itself should be of such a nature that its meaning is not in doubt. Also there should be a thorough education of the people with respect to the whole matter concerning which the plebiscite is being submitted. Then there should be a number of safeguards thrown around the plebiscite to avoid the creeping in of abuses.
So much having been said regarding plebiscites in general, let us turn to the bill before us. This bill in its present form, as I see it, has three main defects. In the first place, it fails to prescribe the length of its own life, and this defect has been laboured by several speakers. Second, it fails to provide for making clear the meaning and significance of the question which is to be put before the people. This also has been dealt with more or less by various speakers. Then, the bill neglects to provide for such adequate education of the people as would enable them completely to apprehend and understand the reason for the plebiscite and the significance of the vote, either yes or no, with respect to the plebiscite.
May I deal with the matter of the length of life of the plebiscite. As the wording in the bill appears-as I think the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out-there is no automatic limitation of the life of the bill; one would say that this is to be a plebiscite bill in general, is to go on the statute books for an indefinite period of time, and is to be a measure under which any administration at any time could hold a plebiscite on any subject whatsoever. The ihon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) reflected upon that situation, and several other speakers have spoken about it. I will grant -that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) specifically stated that the bill was not intended to last long. He said, as reported in Hansard, page 822.
The intention, however, is that the bill should be for one plebiscite only, and that the plebiscite when taken, shall have reference to only one question. That question has -already been made clear to the members of the house and the public, but I will take occasion at once to bring again to -the attention of the house -its exact wording.

I believe we are perfectly safe in saying that the bill as it is must be changed, otherwise there is no legal protection for the Canadian people against any one of several abuses which might creep in as a result of the application of the bill.
As regards the meaning of the plebiscite, the Prime Minister has contended that the meaning is clear. I maintain that, as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) pointed out the other day, this plebiscite is being used throughout Canada as meaning either of two things. It may mean that if one votes "yes", one brings in conscription, or it may mean that he insists that the Prime Minister shall continue without conscription. The plebiscite could be interpreted as meaning no conscription, just as easily as it could be interpreted as meaning conscription.
There is another difficulty which I think I can show some cause for fearing. I turn to page 823 of Hansard and read a passage from the Prime Minister's own speech yesterday. He said:
As I have said, the purpose is to give the government-I put iit in general terms-a perfectly free hand to deal with all matters affecting the war in the manner which, in its judgment, is most in the national interest.
If the Prime Minister's remarks concerning the life of the bill are to be taken as affecting the interpretation of the bill, surely his remarks as to the significance of the bill can likewise be taken as a modifying clause of the meaning of this plebiscite. May I direct the attention of hon. members to another passage of his speech, which they will find on page 826 of Hansard:
This is the issue: Is the government of Canada, in time of war, to have .freedom to take whatever action it thinks most advisable with respect to the furtherance of Canada's war effort?
In that passage, the plebiscite is not particularly limited to the raising of men for overseas service. Let us now turn to page 827 of Hansard, and read:
. . . I feel very strongly the time has come when that limitation should be removed-
The Prime Minister there is talking of the power to conscript for overseas service.
-and when the government should be given the utmost freedom to deal with any phase of the war effort as it thinks best subject always to its responsibility to parliament.

I turn now to page 833 and read the last passage which I shall read in this connection:
In the presentation of the plebiscite to the electorate the desire of the administration to possess complete freedom of action will of course receive the vigorous and wholehearted support of all members of the government. It will, I hope, receive the support of every member of parliament, and will, I believe, receive the support of the Canadian people.
The Prime Minister was there quoting from his speech of January 26, on page 51 of Hansard.
I believe there are sufficient statements there to make it quite clear that this plebiscite can be interpreted to free the government in respect of >far more matters than the raising of men by conscription for overseas service. Some people may say, has the government not all this power under the National Resources Mobilization Act? The government has. But when we remember some of the things that this government has attempted to do under the excuse that they were advantageous to Canada's war effort, one will not hesitate to conclude that there are some things which the rank and file of the people should not interpret as being involved in that act. I refer to the iniquitous recommendations of the Sirois commission. Imagine that, with the statements which are in that speech to give meaning to this plebiscite, the people all over Canada voted "yes"; and the government then declared that the implementing of the report of the Sirois commission was essential to the war effort of Canada; then it would have the mandate of the whole people of Canada to go over the heads of the provinces and implement the recommendations of that report. People may disagree as to the implementing of that report, but I have an idea that when the smoke has cleared away and people realize more fully what that report means, they will certainly not be as much in favour of it as many people have seen fit to be up to the present.
There has been a most dangerous attempt on the part of the government to invade provincial taxation fields, and to do so with the most callous disregard for the commitments, obligations and responsibilities of the provinces. The rebuff which they received in connection with the Sirois report made them a little more cautious, but imagine with what impunity they would go forward if they were backed by a plebiscite such as that upon which we are now going to vote, with the Prime Minister's remarks to give colour to the interpretation of that plebiscite. The wording of the plebiscite should be far more specific and its significance should be far more unmistakable.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Blackmore
The bill should provide for an edequate educational campaign. Upon reading the bill it will be noticed that there is in it no provision whatsoever for the education of the people. Long ago it was said:
Ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
Especially is it necessary for the people of a democracy to know the truth. Throughout this dominion the truth has been withheld, has been garbled, has been distorted in a way that ought to make the public men of Canada for the past several generations hang their heads in shame. To-day we are reaping some of the harvest that was so plentifully sown by the men who distorted the truth. The people must have the truth; otherwise how can they vote intelligently? For example, in many provinces and in many parts of many provinces there is a complete failure to understand this racial problem which goes to the very heart of Canada. There is failure to sympathize with and appreciate the point of view of Canadians who were raised to speak French. As a result, there is bitterness which there never should be and which would be removed if the full truth were known. This bill should provide for educating the people of Canada from coast to coast concerning the races that live in Canada, their numbers, their needs, their preferences and their history. A full account should be given, without reservation, of the shameful appeals that have been made in election campaigns to Canadians who speak French, when men have stooped to sordidness which will forever constitute a stain upon them, to misinform, to inspire with apprehension and anxiety innocent people.
I was much enlightened by two speeches from the other side of the house, one by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. McDonald) and the other by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot). Many hearing them felt that those hon. members were, shall I say, indelicate in having brought out into the open details of the reprehensible behaviour of which Canadians who speak French had been the victims. I never have been able to find any more successful way of adjusting differences between people than the simple method of telling the truth, finding out just why there is misunderstanding. I fail to see why the application of the same principle would not greatly improve conditions in Canada. Here we are, two great races of people, as it were, those whose blood is drawn from French people and those whose blood is drawn from Anglo-Saxons. I think there are no finer peoples in the world to-day than those two races. I find the French-Canadian people
whom I know in every way admirable and estimable, and I see no reason why there should be any prejudice. We are, as it were, two races married. We have a glimpse of ourselves in the midst of a great stream of national life that flows out of a remote past, for which we have no responsibility, and flows into an indefinite future for which we are in some measure responsible. We are similar to a man and wife in a home, with children. We do not wish to break up the home. We do not wish to have a separation or a divorce. If we did wish anything like that, surely a time of such peril as this is not the time to bring the matter to a head. We must come to understand each other. There is only one way in which that can be done; that is, by hearing the facts, sordid as they may be. I can now understand what I have heard men say in this chamber during the four or five years of my sojourn here. I can understand why they have spoken in this way, when I look at the speeches of those two men to whom I have referred. I marvel that the speeches have not been even more extreme.
There should be provision in this bill for an educational campaign from coast to coast, to teach the Canadian people the facts concerning those who dwell with them in this great national household of Canada. The Prime Minister, as reported at page 832 of Hansard, mentioned his desire for an educational campaign, in these words:
I should hope that the campaign would be made lain educational campaign which would help to impress upon the people the necessity of giving the government full power in time of war. I think it can be made that. My hon. friend and I are to-day agreed that the government ought to have this power and we are agreed for the same reason. And the leaders of the other parties are agreed.
But the Prime Minister did not touch what in my judgment is the festering sore which is threatening to break out in eruption, resulting in several kinds of disorder in this country, of which none of us desires even to think. Why not insert in the bill provision for education? While I am referring to this point, may I say that I have never been able to see why the two major parties did not decide to make the last election campaign an educational campaign also. I do not believe the leaders of those parties should be forgiven by generations to come for their neglect to attend to the important matter of educating the people to the truths for which they stand.
When war was declared, in September, 1939, I rose in my place and urged the people concerned that they should go into Quebec
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Blackmore

and tell the truth; everywhere tell the truth. Is it to be conceived that it could not have been made known to every Canadian at that time how colossal was the preparation that Hitler had made, how terrible a foe was Italy, how charged with dynamic explosiveness was the whole Japanese situation? How much more wisely and sanely, and with how much better feeling all would have gone forward if such had been done. Instead of that, what had we? We had an appeal to the basest prejudices, with every attempt to becloud the issues and distort the facts, I presume in every constituency throughout this country. So I say that in this bill there should be specific clauses providing for the setting aside of an adequate fund to provide for the education of the people.
May I turn now from a consideration of the bill to a brief consideration of the Prime Minister's speech. I agree with the leader of the opposition; I do not know whether the Prime Minister has ever delivered a greater speech in his history. It was great, I thought, in every respect. At the same time, he said things which I think should be pointed out. He spoke of the false position in which the government finds itself. I shall leave my hon. friend to explain himself at length some time. If the government wishes to be sure of freeing its hands, then the last thing it ought to have is a plebiscite.
To avoid the possibility of defeat of the plebiscite, which may possibly come about, I am going to make a suggestion, and then I shall have completed my remarks. The people of Canada, from coast to coast, those who are informed and those who think, have begun to realize that there is some sort of dead-hand lying over the whole war effort of this country. I am neither minimizing nor disparaging what the government has done. But it is certain that in a country like Canada, with such bountiful resources, but which at the end of this length of time still has as many unemployed, there is something radically wrong-and simply passing a plebiscite on conscription is not going to set it right. What the people want is that the full, majestic, magnificent strength of this dominion shall be mobilized. People now realize that the devices being used by the government cannot achieve that end, and they are looking for leadership along some new line which will achieve it.
I would suggest to the government even at this late stage that along with the plebiscite in which they are asking if the people are willing that the hands of the government be freed to conscript men for overseas service, if needs be, they ask the further question as to whether the people would be willing to leave the government free so that it could adopt any new financial system which it might find' to be advantageous.
I am going to suggest that the last words in the resolution passed by the legislature of Alberta be given careful attention. Those words were:
The people should be given an opportunity of approving or disapproving not only of the
conscription of man-power but also the complete mobilization of all our material and financial resources through the effective control and issue of all currency and credit by the dominion government.
This was a laughing matter perhaps four years ago. As the days pass, however, the danger that this country will be defeated is increasing, because this matter of money is being neglected. It is by no means a laughing matter to-day, nor can it be taken in any degree lightly. This bill should be redrafted so as to indicate the limit of its life, and to provide for adequate education; and the plebiscite should be revised so as to make its meaning and significance explicit. It should also contain facilities to enable the people to express their opinions on monetary systems.
