speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I have been a member of the House of Commons I have found it to be a place of very much kindness. While I am here I hope I shall never be charged with showing any lack of ordinary Christian charity toward those who sit round me or hon. gentlemen opposite. To-day we are passing through a great battle of nerves, and the affairs of state place a heavy strain on the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the cabinet and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson).
The government, however, should not be afraid to tell the people when they have made a mistake because, as I have said on former occasions, the people do not expect their leaders to be gods. There has never been a question in Canada concerning which all people have ever been united, and that arises because of our population and other matters. The plebiscite question is one on which different views are held.
Before discussing the plebiscite in detail, may I compliment Mr. Speaker, Mr. Deputy Speaker and the splendid Clerk of the House upon the very kind and efficient way in which they have handled the proceedings of the house in these critical times. They have done their duty as they have seen it, and I believe they have won the admiration and respect of the members and the people of Canada. Tme it is that sometimes I did not agree with them, but the fact that I say so, does not make it so.
Next December 9 it will have been twenty-one years since I was first elected to this house. As I say I have found that the house has discussed all these questions in a calm way. There is no necessity for anybody getting rattled at the present time over the questions that are before us. I am one of the opposition, but I believe the opposition

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Church
has given the government pretty good independent support in this war. That is what we were sent here for, to offer criticism, on behalf of the man on the street, on behalf of the people in our constituencies and the people of Canada generally. They may not like the way in which the war is going on, but it is no disparagement of the Prime Minister, of any of his ministers or of the government of the day if criticism is offered.
I believe in the parliamentary system. They do not believe in it in Germany and Japan, but in this country we have a parliamentary system in a democracy. There cannot be a democracy without a free press. That is why I have urged the government to abolish the censorship as they have done in England. If that had been done, we would have avoided many of the mistakes which have been made in the giving of news and information to the people.
I think I have known the Prime Minister longer than anyone else in this house, and I have never had anything but respect for him while he has held his present position. I also have a great deal of admiration for the leader of the opposition. This party was not disgraced in the last election because it polled nearly one-half of the total vote in the country. Our leader was defeated, and the hon. member for York-Sunbury took up this work and has done well. He has not been very well, and his conduct of this job has won him the respect and admiration, not only of his colleagues over here but, I believe, on all sides of the house. He has won considerable public estimation in the country. He is not here at present this evening. Probably if he were, I would not be saying this, but it is true.
As I said in the first speech I made when this present parliament was opened in 1940, and when the government were being criticized, after all is said and done the people have elected them. They won 178 seats and they are the government of the day in a democracy. The people put them there. As I said at that time, they were a government of Canadians in Canada. Aside from the question of man-power, which they have misjudged, I think they have done a great deal of good useful work. Their efforts so far have been considerable, and Canada's war effort is very creditable in many ways, but they have not done one-half of what they should have done nor enough for a total war effort. They misjudged things in connection with man-power, in connection with the European and Pacific situation, in connection with the disarmament movement before the war. The members of the opposi-

tion have endeavoured to give the government good and independent support on the whole, for a total effort. The government has very little about which to complain except on this one question of the plebiscite, which never should have been started.
This is an involved question and one cannot expect everybody to agree. We are not all constituted the same. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I am a little shortsighted.
I can speak without notes for forty mintues, but I have a few short quotations I should like to make. I did not want to bring in a lot of books, so I have these quotations tjqpewritten in my notes.
One thing has been shown since the start of the war-the tremendous popularity of the monarchy. We had evidence of this during the visit of the king and queen in May, 1939, and again, last December on the king's birthday. The king and queen have been most magnificent in giving leadership in these critical war days. As I say, one of the cardinal things we have noticed in Canada is the popularity of the monarchy, but with that we have seen the decay of parliament and the decline of the House of Commons. This is evidenced by the mistakes that have been made in allowing our functions to be usurped. We come here for a few days; then the doors are locked and we go home. Our colleagues in another place have been here for four or five hours since last June. Why can we not follow the example of London and W ashington and have a joint session of the two houses, as I urged here in 1939 and 1940? This is what should be done during the course of this greatest war in the history of the world. But nothing has been done. Some very good talent is to be found in the other part of this building, men of great experience and ability, but no use has been made of their services in connection with wTar work. That is one of the mistakes which have been made.
I do not mean any disparagement when I say that the Prime Minister has been conducting this war as a Liberal war. The Asquith government went out of office in England during the last war for the same reason. The conduct of this war is much more difficult than was the conduct of the great war, and I think the Prime Minister would have been well advised to have hearkened to the hand-writing on the wall. Instead of conducting the war in the way in which it has been conducted, we should have had a man like Lord Beaverbrook or

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Church
used the great talents and ability of Viscount Bennett in the war cabinet in London. We all know the wonderful work that Lord Beaverbrook has done in production in the old land. He was bom at Maple in York, although he is considered to be a Nova Scotian. I was sorry that he did not accompany the Prime Minister of Great Britain when he came here. Lord Beaverbrook is a remarkable man and a great Canadian. Considerable could be done in London by way of better managing of our part of this war. This is not the battle of the Atlantic; it is the battle of the seven seas, and there must be a new management of our own war effort. This has been shown by results in the Pacific. When the Right Hon. Mr. Menzies addressed this chamber last June he pointed this out. The government knew about it; they could see the hand-writing on the wall, but nothing was done till too late, and the disaster there shocked the world.
The government are a board of directors appointed by the people to conduct the war. The responsibility is theirs. It is a difficult job, and I sometimes fear for the health of some of the leaders. The strain they undergo ' is one of the tragedies of this game, and I hope it will not injure their health.
On the second reading the principle of the bill is considered. This is set out in the splendid textbook I hold in my hand, Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms. I remember reading what the assistant clerk, now the clerk of the British House of Commons said about this textbook. Standing order 75, at page 216, deals with the second reading. I should like to quote citation 753, which reads:
The second reading of a bill is that stage when it is proper to enter into a discussion and propose a motion relative to the principle of the measure.
Citation 755 reads:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution; or otherwise opposed to its progress; or seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees, commissioners, the production of papers or other evidence or the opinion of judges.
For that reason I oppose the principle of this bill. I should like to point out the cause and effect of this bill. What has been the cause for this sudden departure from parliamentary institutions and all we have had here for over one hundred years? As I said the other day, a civil war was fought in England
over the very principle involved in this plebiscite, the control of the executive by parliament. In my opinion the cause for this plebiscite was simply a smoke-screen, a bit of shadow-boxing to cover up the mistakes which have been made about man-power since the war started and the disaster in the Pacific. It is simply a smoke-screen to cover the Pacific and Singapore. Who proposed this plebiscite? Who asked for it? What will it cost? It will do nothing whatever to beat Hitler.
I was very much disappointed with the speech which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), who is not here to-night, made in this house on February 4. The government can spend all this money like water on a useless plebiscite and on the league but has not a dollar to pay the poor dependents, the wives and children of the soldiers, many of whom are suffering from lack of a bonus, from lack of fuel and all that kind of thing. Yet the Minister of Finance brings down a page and a half of an order in council to give a cost of living bonus to civil servants who are staying at home and not going to the war. In addition to their $175 a month, they are being given a war bonus, and we cannot get a dollar for the dependents of the soldiers, or free fares for the soldiers on the railways, or a national insurance scheme. History will score this disgraceful treatment of our forces.
This plebiscite will not amount to a thing in beating Hitler. The effect of it will be like the effect of all commissions and committees in this country-to kill a lot of time, and delay and hinder and prevent this House of Commons from fulfilling the function for which it was created and urging upon the government an increased war effort. This is no time for such a reference to the people, and the plebiscite has already done a lot of harm in this country. I was sorry to hear some of the language used in this house to-night by two most honoured and respected leaders. I know that it was done in the heat of debate and that the battle of nerves is pretty hard1 on both of them, but I was sorry to see it.
If Hitler comes here-and he is not far from our shores now-he will take no plebiscite. What he will do will be to hang the plebiscite and all connected with it on a sour apple tree, like John Brown's body. That is what he will do with it, and Hitler and Japan are not, 1 repeat, far from our shores now. When the members representing British Columbia constituencies urged the government to do something to solve the Japanese question out there, why, on the same plebiscite reasoning, did the government not hold a plebiscite on the question of moving these Japanese-twenty-
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Church

eight or thirty thousand at the maximum and twenty thousand at the minimum-away from the coast province? It did not hold a plebiscite on that because the members would not stand for it.
This vote will probably be taken in May or June, which are going to be two of the most fateful months the world has ever seen. In those months will be decided the fate of civilization, perhaps for the next two hundred years. It will not be home defence that will count then. The decisive battles will be fought in the Atlantic and the Pacific, in Asia, and Europe, and the Mediterranean. In the Pacific we have lost the command of the sea and you cannot keep up with the Japanese who are moving around to these various islands in the Pacific-no, not if you had one million men, as I quoted Mr. Churchill early in the session. * They have command of the air, aeroplane carriers, all the deadly instruments of war and have battered the fleets of Britain and the United States in the Pacific. The danger to the people of this country is great. Our fate will be decided, not by home defence, but in the Pacific; in the battle of the Atlantic, which is really a misnomer because it should be called the battle of the seven seas; and in the Mediterranean and on the Russo-German front, whether we like it or not. They can go like a circus from place to place with sea and air supremacy.
You cannot conduct this war with a plebiscite. It must be conducted by the House of Commons. Under the constitution you must either support the government or oppose it, and you cannot change the constitution by a plebiscite. The members of the House of Commons have not only the right but the duty to come here and report what they find wrong with our war effort and in connection with our armed forces and economic effort, and I say the critics have been right. It is their duty to point out what is wrong.
On the second reading of the bill you can discuss the principle, but you cannot discuss the bill in detail clause by clause. The interpretation clause provides that "during a plebiscite" means the period between the date of the proclamation ordering the plebiscite issued under section 3 of this act, and the close of the poll on polling day. That is what the definition says about the time of the plebiscite. But if Hitler comes to this country first, what are you going to do about it? He will not hold any plebiscite. He did not hold one in Belgium or Holland or France and these other countries he has conquered.

By clause 3 of the bill it is provided that the governor-in-council "may" by proclamation order the taking of a plebiscite. The "may" is enabling, permissive; it is not mandatory. The governor in council has control of the plebiscite election. But if Hitler or the Japanese come here, there will be no vote at all, because the govemor-in-council can call it off then, or at any time.
Section 5 of the bill provides that any person who shall have voted at the plebiscite shall not be exempted from military training. That smacks of conscription, and it is conscription. There is no such provision in the statute which Attorney-General Conant brought down in the Ontario legislature for soldier votes abroad and at home. He has given a free and untrammelled right of way to all the soldiers overseas and all those wearing the service uniform to vote at the next election. He is not taking away from them by conscriptive methods anything at all as we are, their right to apply for exemption, postponement of training, and all that kind of thing.
Another section of the bill provides that members of the forces, irrespective of age, shall be entitled to vote on the plebiscite. Another section deals with the manner of voting by a qualfied voter whose name is not on the official list of voters. Anybody who knows anything about elections, especially in districts where there is a foreign-born population, knows that this will lead to a lot of telegraphing of votes. Persons will be going round to various booths and voting if their names are not on the lists. I remember an election once where the candidate got 178 votes at one poll, but the "8" was struck off, so that this candidate got only 17 votes. I do not like to see that kind of thing, and voting by those not on the lists.
When the seed planted by this plebiscite has reached its maturity, what will the harvest be? It will not fill the farmers' barns with crops. It will empty their pockets of their money, and their taxes will pay for it. All the harvest will be that the people will not know what they are voting on, and when the votes are counted up, half the ballots will be spoiled because the people did not know what they were voting on. It puts me in mind of the battle of Dundee. I see the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) sitting over there with his colleague. They know about the battle of Dundee where no one knew who won it. Some say we won; some say they won; some say nobody won- and that is how it will be when the plebiscite ballots are counted.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Church
It is not right to place private government members of parliament in the position in which this plebiscite places them, against their own convictions. We are being asked to relieve the government of responsibility for policy by submitting to the people a plebiscite asking them to vote "yes" or "no." It is parliament's duty to frame policy; and if we are not here for that, the government had better lock the doors of this house and send the members home for good.
A "yes" vote is simply a vote of entire confidence in the government. I do not know whether I shall Vote or not. My constituents have the right to vote the way they see fit, and it is not for me to advise or interfere with them. I am not going to be a party to any snap or humbug vote or anything in the nature of a vote when the people do not know what they are voting for. They do not know what will happen if they vote "yes", or what will happen if they vote "no"; they are bewildered. To the average voter the thing is a genuine Chinese puzzle without any issue or sense. What is going to be the result of it? What was the cause of it?
Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said that conscription is not an issue in this vote, that the issue is a pledge of the government. Let me remind him that Mr. Roosevelt, the President of the United States, gave a pledge in the last election that there would never be a contingent of troops sent out of the country if he were returned; he would stop at measures just short of war and they would keep out of war. What happened? Last June he carried the army vote by a majority of only one. The isolationists were so strong that the majority for the repeal of the Neutrality Act was only fourteen votes. Things looked pretty dark for the administration until Pearl Harbour changed the whole situation and the whole nation was united. Are we going to wait to take a plebiscite until we have a second Pearl Harbour in Victoria or Vancouver; because, as Prime Minister Churchill told the House of Commons in London publicly the other day-it was reported in Hansard of January 28 there-for the next year or two, until the allies get command of the sea in the Pacific again, we must expect these visits from the enemy in the Pacific, and for Japan to roam all over. Are we to wait until then before we do anything?
So much for the bill. My leader is quite correct in what he says about the plebiscite as being contrary to the constitution. I have here an authority for my statement-and I shall quote it in a moment-because this .matter has been up in the house before. This
particular plebiscite method of doing business is subversive of our constitution, which is derived from that of Great Britain. It takes away the collective responsibility of the cabinet of the day and cabinet solidarity. Instead of the public being approached through a plebiscite, the issue should have been embodied in a government measure in the house here, and if rejected, the government falls. I believe the house would have released the government from any pledge in this connection. Why are they worrying about pledges? I do not know. As the late J. Israel Tarte said, elections are not won with prayers, and platforms are made to get in on, not to stand on-and so are pledges.
I might point out that the Prime Minister, when replying to me in 1937 concerning a national register, gave a. pledge in this house that the government would never again send overseas an expeditionary force; he said that the danger to Canada was minor in degree and secondary in origin-which statement is shown to have been incorrect. In addition, what did he do in the Atlantic conference, which binds Canada whether we like it or not? At the last imperial conference, in 1937, when we refused to give anything to the Singapore base, or support an empire shipping policy, although it meant more to Canada than almost any other country in the way of protection in the Pacific, he said, "We have no commitments. Parliament will decide." How was the pledge carried out?
Take the Hyde Park and Ogdensburg agreements. We have a so-called joint board of defence, which is more board than defence; in fact, it seems to be all board. That body has made recommendations of expenditures running to two or three hundred million dollars- all over the head of parliament, although we are in session. In the Hyde Park agreement are pledges binding on Canada, also the giving away of bases from Newfoundland to British Guiana and elsewhere. In return for fifty ships, some of which have been returned, and others of which are very little use, we gave away parts of our empire. This binds Canada, although it was not a party to it.
At the Atlantic conference they decided that we would be at war if war came to the United States and Japan; Britain would join the United States, and that bound Canada. We have never yet had a defence or foreign policy. We have never yet had a foreign policy except a policy of day to day and hand to mouth. These commitments which are being made between the governments of Great Britain and the United States bind Canada, because when Britain is at war, Canada is at war.
8S4
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Church

I do not agree with the head of that high-sounding Department of National War Services, which with all its circuitous ways should have been abolished long ago, when he allows Mr. Brockington to make such statements in literature as these: "King George did not declare war for us; we declared war for him."
When war broke out on September 3, 1939, although it took ten days for this parliament to declare war, Hitler did not wait for our declaration of war of September 10; he sank the Athenia on September 3, with a hundred and thirty Canadians and other Britishers on board. It needed' no declaration from us to become involved, because when Britain is at war, Canada is at war also. Another instance of a pledge which has not been carried out is the Ogdensburg agreement.
Then, more recently, how was war declared on Japan? I had asked the Prime Minister on June 12 last whether, during the parliamentary recess, there was to be any further appeasement of Japan. He said he was not an appeaser, he was a conciliator. Under the appeasement policy Japan received from us five million bushels of grain. One of those who spoke in connection with that particular subject when Japan declared war on December 7 was the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), who for many years supported pacifist doctrines and resisted even the moderate votes which were proposed for armaments in 1937 and 1938. He gave a long interview last December to the press about Japan, in which, according to him, Japan could not last any time at all. His prediction has proved to be incorrect and his facts out of date or judgment.
I come to this point. During the time we were giving away the Ottawa valley and other power rights, allowing increases in telephone rates, and when large vested interests were threatening municipal control over streets, it was proposed to adopt in Canada the municipal policy of submitting to the ratepayers at every general election great national questions in peace time. In this connection I would refer to what was said by the late honoured Secretary of State, Mr. Rinfret, in corroboration of what our leader has said. A report of the discussion will be found in Hansard of March 17, 1939, page 2186. The constitutional aspects of the matter were debated; and it was pointed out, in relation to an act of June 13, 1898, respecting the prohibition of importation and manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors, that a vote was all right; but there was no legislation, although Sir Wilfrid Laurier had pledged legislation.
I recall an occasion when Sir Wilfrid, who was very popular with those who came to interview

him, saw that one member of a delegation did not have a chair, and he would not sit down himself but got the delegate a chair. His name was the Reverend Mr. Huxtable, who addressed him as "Sir Wilfrid." Sir Wilfrid said, "Don't call me Sir Wilfrid; I am plain Mr. Laurier, a democrat to the hilt." But a few months afterwards Sir Wilfrid forgot his pledge and took a knighthood-quite rightly and quite properly; he was held in very affectionate regard and respect by the people not only of his own province but of others.
The Secretary of State pointed out what the government did after the vote to which I have referred was held. What they did was to place the Canada Temperance Act on the statute books of a later day. It provided for local referendums, and under that act the Secretary of State of that day said that some two hundred separate local votes were held throughout the country and in Ontario and Manitoba. The late Minister of Justice, the very able and respected minister whom we all miss so much this session, opposed plebiscites on March 17, 1939, and he gave some reasons for not applying it to federal matters at general elections. He said it could not be applied in an emergency. I told my leader some years ago on referendums that if war came, I would never see Mr. General Election become commander in chief of the British forces; I would never with my vote allow Mr. General Election to become admiral of the British fleet, because before Mr. General Election could open his ballot boxes, the enemy would sail and fly up the St. Lawrence and bomb the citadel at Quebec and this building and the Chateau Laurier hotel. I am1 still of that opinion. My present leader is absolutely correct in saying that the plebiscite is contrary to the constitution and that the matter should be dealt with by way of a special act and not a general act, because under the Dominion Elections Act you cannot submit a question, and that is why they have to bring in this bill. It will have to go to the senate, and I shall be very much surprised if it does not get a rough reception in another place.
In 1939 the then Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret), pointed out the time this referendum will take. There are no standing lists in Ottawa; it will take seven or eight weeks to prepare them. I think it was Mr. Devlin in the home rule debate who said the House of Commons was at its best when it was frank. We want some frankness from the government as to the management of this war-the better management. It is the duty of this house to be frank and to criticize the measures placed before it, because criticism is a tonic to government action. This government has refused

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Church
to do anything in regard to some of the main measures but was urged on by public opinion. It was so in regard to man-power and many articles of munitions and in many other ways.
I believe that the man on the street has a right to be heard here in criticism. In my opinion the criticism by the opposition has been very moderate. The man in the street has a right to 'be heard and the only way he can be heard is through a member of parliament, because the private member is the connecting link between the government of the day and the electorate; if he ceases to function, parliamentary government is at an end. If the press is to be muzzled by censors on this plebiscite then the public is not going to learn the facts.
I for one do not intend to fall into this plebiscite trap. I know something about the conduct of elections and the mysterious and devious ways sometimes used to win them, and I am opposed to it. I am not going to be manoeuvred into a wrong position by the jokers in this bill, and there are many of them. I am not going to be told to put a cross "yes" or "no" to any' such question, or to be a party to such tomfoolery. I have seen too much manipulation of ballot boxes in my day, and I never had much organization, no more than any of the other Toronto members; we have had very little organization except in a voluntary way.
The people do not believe in this plebiscite. The Prime Minister evidently looks on it as a straight vote of confidence; if you vote "yes," you vote confidence. Mr. Churchill asked for a vote of confidence, but he asked for it in the right way, in the House of Commons under the constitution, and that is the way it should be done here.
The government may get a surprise in the ballot boxes. With regard to the referendum or plebiscite-it is a distinction without a difference, a play on words-I believe the people are not going to be fooled. You can fool some of the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time as to an important matter like this, especially when it means life or death with the enemy close to our shores.
In 1937 I predicted the war over Japan on a vote for the Tokyo legation, and my late leader Viscount Bennett said I represented a large body of public opinion in this country that did not like the way in which Canada had been for many years a drag on the mother country. As I said in that debate, one of our chief errors was the refusal to cooperate with the motherland in connection with Singapore and the shipping conference.
Britain at that time had two thousand fewer ships than in 1914 and five million more mouths to feed.
Conscription was not an issue in the last election. I never heard of it; in fact I had a difference of opinion with one of our leaders about this question. I did not speak in the last election except in my own constituency, and no leader is going to tie me down. I am not a yes-man or a nodder, or a follow your leader; your leader is your policy; I never have been and do not intend to be now. It is a great mistake for the present Prime Minister to ask his followers to agree with him on this and no government member should be placed in this position.
The Prime Minister asked the question and gave the answer. I have the answer here. The question was "to release the government" from its pledge. I am in favour of striking out all the words after "release the government". If he will have the question read: "Are you in favour of releasing the government?" to be answered by a straight "yes" or "no", the people would understand. If the Prime Minister is appealing to Caesar, let him appeal and be bound by the answer.
If there were a little more humour in the house, tempers would not be so frayed or rattled. I think this plebiscite is unsportsmanlike. I was at a rugby game not long ago, where there were some five thousand people; one side began to yell, "We don't like the ref, we don't like the ref", meaning the referee. We do not like the referendum. The men are all right. I look on this vote as war according to Hollywood and not war according to Hitler. The people are not going to be fooled by any such farce. I have seen voters in the voting booths decline to vote on such similar questions because they do not like to be humbugged and did not understand them. The average voter knows as much as members of the House of Commons and the cabinet; he does not need any meetings to tell him how to vote. I think it is an insult to ask members of parliament to go to the constituencies and pull the chestnuts out of the fire for the government on such a proposal. I do not intend to do it; my constituents can vote themselves as they see fit. I do not know whether I am going to vote myself on the question, because I took a stand in this house for rearmament all along the line when it was very unpopular and not fashionable, and it is very unwise now for some hon. members to throw cheap sneers at those who in season and out of season, for years before the war, urged a larger army, navy and air force.
8S6
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Church

The German barbarians with their mechanized hordes have destroyed the whole of Europe, and they are not far from our shores now. I do not think you are going to fool any of the people at the ballot box by this sort of thing. Before the ballot boxes can be opened the enemy may arrive on the Pacific or the Atlantic coast, with the tramping of feet, the loud speaker, the cracking of the whip, the sergeant-major, the gestajpo, and all that sort of thing. He may decide the matter long before the ballot boxes are opened. I like the bon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght); he has been very kind to everyone, but I do not like some of his arguments about the ballot on the plebiscite. Neither do I like those of his young friend, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford), who sits beside him. I think it would be far better if in future he used a little more temperate language with regard to those who do not agree with him. I hope it may never be said of me that in my twenty-one years in this house I ever failed to show a lack of ordinary Christian charity toward my political opponents.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not so far availed myself of the opportunity to speak on this plebiscite issue. Much has been said about it since the opening of parliament some weeks ago. I think I can agree with some of those who have already eulogized the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on his speech yesterday. I believe he is a past master at saying a great deal, yet so speaking as to avoid any possibility of being pinned down. Sometimes I think he is rather like a jack rabbit; just when you think you have him, he is not there. I quite agree with those who have expressed the opinion that yesterday he excelled himself in oratory and forcefulness, and as he was speaking I felt that if only he had made that speech during the early part of this session, instead of waiting until yesterday, he might have saved a great deal of time. Sometimes, however, first impressions are best, and I believe that as we seriously analyse the Prime Minister's speech of yesterday we may discover some things that perhaps he overlooked or some things that perhaps he did not very brilliantly cover up.
Yesterday the right hon. gentleman said that the question he was going to ask the public to answer in this plebiscite was as follows:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I think this question is so ambiguous that it is not capable of

even- one interpretation. Some hon. members have said that it is capable of many interpretations, but I cannot interpret it at all. Already under the mobilization act the government has perfect freedom; it is not restricted at all in its method of raising men for military service. That has nothing at all to do with the restriction. Where the government is restricted is in respect of where the men who are raised should fight the war. I want to point that out, because we have been told here, and the Prime Minister made the statement himself, that this plebiscite has nothing whatever to do with conscription. Yet all our arguments have centred around whether or not the government could con-soript men for overseas service. Therefore the government is not restricted as to the methods of raising men for military service, but rather as to the purpose for which the men who are raised for military service should be used. Are they going to be raised to serve at home, or are they going to be raised to serve abroad? But that is not contained in the question which is to be submitted to the people.	So I say, Mr. Speaker, that the question is so very ambiguous that personally I do not know what it does mean. I should like to ask the Prime Minister what it means. He says that it does not mean the conscription of men for overseas service; yet throughout his speech yesterday	he continually mentioned the
matter of overseas service.
When the Prime Minister mentioned yesterday the question that was to be submitted to the people, he went on to say this, as it appears at page 823 of Hansard:
As I said, at the time of speaking on the address, the question is very simple in its language and meaning and is a straightforward one.
Yet a few lines further down, in almost the next breath, he went on to say:
My purpose this afternoon is not so much to attempt ito add to what has been said but rather, if possible, to clear away some of the confusion that has arisen out of the discussion that has already taken place.
If the question we have been debating is couched in language so straightforward that there can be no doubt about it, how is it that confusion exists? That is one point at least on which the Prime Minister did not cover up so brilliantly as he is accustomed to do.
Let me go a step further. Yesterday the Prime Minister took time out to mention specifically that there is a tremendous difference between a legal obligation and a moral obligation. I wonder whether there was any

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hansell
moral obligation in 1940, in going to the people with a promise of restriction. I wonder whether there was any moral obligation in going to the country and saying, "We want j'ou to return us to power so that we can prosecute the war so far but no farther." If ever there was a moral obligation, it was in 1940, when the Prime Minister went to the country; and the moral obligation was to tell the people that he was going to do anything under God's heaven to win the war. But I think he went to the country with only one moral obligation in mind, and that was to win the election.
Later on in the Prime Minister's speech he makes special reference to the fact that both Conservative and Liberal parties, the two major parties of Canada, going to the country in 1940, were in agreement on the matter of voluntary enlistment and1 compulsory enlistment; that is, the matter of conscription.
Then he deals with the pledge that was made to the country. Let me read the Prime Minister's words:
The pledge was given later, direct to the people, to the electorate themselves. It was a pledge made between the leaders of two great political parties in Canada and the electorate of this country in regard to the most solemn question that could have been put before them at that particular time.
The Prime Minister specifically states that this was the most solemn pledge that could be given the country. I repeat-the most solemn pledge. The most solemn pledge any man could give the country in a time of war is the pledge to win the war at all costs. That is the most solemn pledge which could be given.
But what was the pledge that was considered1 so solemn? It was: We will prosecute this war in order to win the war at home; but we will not prosecute the war to the very limit of our capacity to win it abroad. That is the sort of pledge the Prime Minister regards as a solemn one.

Some of us could say a few things about solemn pledges. Here again, talking about public men in public positions, and how they must regard their pledges as solemn and irrevocable, the Prime Minister goes on to say:
We intend to be ever mindful of this, and that if we have given a solemn pledge to them we intend to carry out that pledge.
That sounds good; it sounds beautiful. But might I ask the Prime Minister about the solemn pledge he made a few years ago to end unemployment?

speechtext: He never made it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I believe I remember reading in Maclean's magazine about October, 1935, where the Prime Minister was going to ease the burden of debt on agriculture. Did he ease the burden of debt? Did he go to the country and ask to be released from that solemn promise? In this house in the last year or two we have been reminded that the farmers in Saskatchewan were promised dollar wheat. The government was not able to give the farmers dollar wheat. Was that a solemn pledge? Has the government asked release from that pledge?
Then I would remind the house once again of that most solemn pledge respecting the issue of currency and credit in terms of public need. We know what the Prime Minister said in 1935; these words have almost been worn threadbare:
Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury once in control will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government, and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament is idle and futile.
The Prime Minister talks about keeping solemn pledges. Here is one he has described as a sacred responsibility. I do not know what the broad meaning of the word "sacred" is, but I have before me the meaning as it appears in a dictionary I secured in the parliamentary library. The meaning of "sacred" as outlined here is "consecrated, or held dear to a deity; dedicated or reserved or appropriated to some person or purpose; made holy by religious issue; hallowed."
Let us think of that. Here is a sacred responsibility, one which is consecrated1 or held dear to a deity. Did the Prime Minister keep that most sacred obligation? Has he restored to the government the right to issue currency and credit in terms of public need?
I should like to read something he said on the night of the election, when Mr. Bennett's government was swept out and Mr. King's government was swept in. In the light of what has gone on since, in the light of
Plebiscite Act

Mr. Hansell

the fact that millions of people have been, on relief, let me read what the Prime Minister said:
In the new era which dawns to-day the struggle for the rights of the people will, in the realm of economic liberty and security, be carried on as never before.

Poverty and adversity, want and misery are the enemies which Liberalism will seek to oanish from our land. No time must be lost.

speechtext: The question before the house has to do with a plebiscite.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: 1 am the last one who would want to break any of the rules of this house. If, however, you had been in the chair this afternoon you would have heard members here and members there talk their way around the world and half way to the moon and still be permitted to go on and speak. I want you to rule, Mr. Speaker, but I am saying that if there ever was a sacred obligation or pledge which the Prime Minister has ever made and which should have been kept-if it could not be kept, he should have submitted the matter to the people by way of a plebiscite-it was the pledge to end suffering and want in the midst of plenty.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: He did not want to do it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) says that he did not want to do it; it did not suit his political convenience. Imagine the Prime Minister going to the country in those days with a plebiscite asking that he be released from
[Mr. Hansell.1
his obligation to end poverty when he found he could not do it. That would not have suited his political convenience, but this plebiscite does. May I go on with the Prime Minister's speech of yesterday. He is reported on page 826 of Hansard as follows:
It is because of this we want to have perfect freedom of action as an administration, to have all the right to do what is in the public interest at the time the situation may demand iit, and we feel we ought to be given this freedom as quickly as possible. The reason we want it, as I have stated already, is to be free to act in the manner which will best serve the interests of the people of Canada to serve in the manner that will make Canada's war effort the most effective.
That is self-admission that in 1940, when he made the commitment, it was a commitment which restricted him from putting forth Canada's greatest possible war effort. Are we to understand that the government went to this country in a time of war, in 1940, with the attitude that they did not want to be free to prosecute this war to the limit of their ability? In effect the Prime Minister says that they went to the country in 1940 with no desire to be free to carry on the war in the most effective manner. The only conclusion one can come to for the government permitting its hands to be tied is that it considered it was a very good piece of political expediency. I cannot comprehend it; it is beyond imagination, beyond all reason to believe that the government should consult the people as to whether they desire it to take such action as will win the war. That is the line of argument the Prime Minister used. He goes on:
Hon. members have been talking about conscription, about no conscription and the like. That is no-t the issue in this plebiscite. This is the issue: Is the government of Canada, in time of war, to have freedom to take whatever action it thinks most advisable with respect to the furtherance of Canada's war effort?
The Prime Minister informed the house that the question to be submitted to the people is not whether or not they want conscription, but whether or not they want the government to do all they can do to win the war. I am not going through my constituency doffing a cap with bells on, looking like a fool, asking my constituents to vote whether or not they want to win the war. Then the Prime Minister goes on to talk about the position in which the government finds itself in the eyes of the world.
He said:
First of all, the government is being put in an entirely wrong position before the people of this country and before the world just because we have not that full power.
8S9

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hansell
Who put them in that position except he himself in 1940? Again on page 827:
. . . but it is also putting Canada in a false position, before all countries of the world, including her allies in the war.
Who put Canada in that position but themselves in 1940? I quote from page 826: Nevertheless as long as that commitment is there we are being represented to the people of our own and other countries as a government unwilling to go the lengths other countries are willing to go, even should necessity for so doing become clearly manifest. That is a false position and a very wrong one in which to have the government placed.
Moreover, the present position in regard to the one commitment places the parliament of Canada, as well, in a false position.
Who put the government in that position but they themselves in 1940? If I have not misjudged what the Prime Minister says, it is that parliament is being put in a false position. I quote from page 827:
The very minute the subject were brought up, one hon. member after another, if it suited his purpose, would rise in his place in the house and say, "I cannot discuss this question, because the government is committed not even to raise it." So long as that commitment is there, no matter how the war may develop, there can be no discussion of the merits of the question of compulsory service for overseas. I say that that is putting parliament in a wrong position before the people of Canada.
It seems to me that the Prime Minister must think it is a Liberal parliament. Is he going to say that nobody in the house can talk about conscription until the government raises the issue? That is the way it reads here. I have thought for some time that this is a Liberal parliament. That is the position. Then he says:
. . . the enemy will construe this commitment as a limitation on the war effort of Canada.
What is responsible for that? I wonder how they interpreted that commitment in Germany in 1940?

speechtext:
That is exactly the argument I am making, that it was political expediency. On page 828, the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
Talk about being courageous, I do not see anything courageous about that. Courage comes when you face the people, not when you run away from them.
A little more courage in 1940 would have been wise. It would have been better if he had faced the country with the statement, not "I will not put in conscription," but modified a little to read, "I see no need for conscription now, but if the need ever comes, I shall be the first to put it in." That would have been courageous indeed.
The Prime Minister answered the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) to the effect that he could not state what he would do in respect of conscription as a result of the plebiscite vote, and he could not state what he would do several months hence. But he did state in 1940 what he could not do and would not do- and that condition has lasted for two years. The Prime Minister said, as reported at page 831 of Hansard of yesterday:
I mention these things because they help to illustrate how impossible it is for .the government to give a decision here and now as to what it is going to do next September or. October or November or December, or in 1943 or 1944.
I am not pressing that he should tell us that.
I am simply pointing out that he did tell the country in 1940 what he could not do and would not do. He went to the country then on a negative commitment, and I say and have always thought that it was one of the most foolish things for a statesman to do to go to the country and say: I am promising you that if you elect me I will not do something, but will go into office with my hands tied. That may have been a shrewd piece of political expediency, but I do not think I will apologize to the Prime Minister when I say that it was not statesmanlike.
The Prime Minister went on in his speech to talk about the New Order. It is true that he wound up his speech with a great finale. It is worth putting on Hansard twice. The Prime Minister said, as reported at page 833 of Hansard:
A great deal has been said in different parts of the world and in our own country, about the New Order that is to come when this war is over. I have said on two or three occasions, I feel it very deeply', that unless that New Order emerges and asserts itself before the war is over we shall see very litle of New Order when the war is over.
Might I just make some reference to that? The Prime Minister makes that statement in the sense that he wants to preserve democracy, wants the people's will to govern. He says so here, as reported at page 834 of yesterday's Hansard:
They will insist on public honour in the transaction of public business, and they will insist above everything else that the government that is carrying on the affairs of their country shall be responsive to the will of the people and see that it is administering that will and no other.
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hansell

Will the Prime Minister tell me to-night if it is the will of the Canadian people to pay an old age pension of only $20 a month? Will he tell me that it is the will of the people that agriculture should get the deal it is getting and that soldiers' widows should get the deal they are getting? The government knows the will of the people on these things.
The Prime Minister goes on to say, as reported at page 834 of yesterday's Hansard-.
There has been very little said in the recent past about moral obligations on the part of nations,^ but unless I am greatly mistaken there is nothing that is going to mean as much in the future of mankind. If we are going to rule out of our public life the honour of public men and of parliament-
And so forth, and so on, and so on, and so on. Yes, there are sacred obligations, and statesmen should keep their commitments. I believe in that. But there are sacred' obligations to feed and clothe and make our people happy and comfortable. That is the will of the people, but that is not being done to-day.
Speaking of the post-war period, the Prime Minister goes on to say, as reported at page 835 of Hansard:
We are going to honour their rights as we seek to honour our own conscience, so we shall be laying the foundation of the kind of order that will be enduring through the years to come.
Then I say, let us start with the building of that foundation now by looking after these war widows and dependents, and let us look after the aged now, for these are sacred and solemn obligations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the arguments that have been made in the debate on the address and in this debate with respect to the plebiscite, pro and con, and also to the arguments for and against conscription. I am firmly convinced that before the plebiscite is put to the people, the first step we should take is this: We should have a resolution moved in this House of Commons by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) asking the members of this house to relieve the Prime Minister of his pledge. Most of the members who have spoken said that they were in favour of the plebiscite, but they have not said what they are going to do. They have not said whether they will back it up, whether they will ask their people to vote for it or whether they themselves' will actually vote for it or not. To ask the people first, instead of this House of Commons, is putting the cart before the horse. I am not in favour of the plebiscite; I think the Prime Minister can get the release he requires from the members of this House of Commons; and before he submits the plebiscite to the people of the country,

he should secure his release from the members of the House of Commons. If he gets release there, he certainly will be much freer to act than he is now; and if some unforeseen terrible thing shojild happen to prevent the taking of the plebiscite, he will at least have the consent of the members of the House of Commons to relieve him of his obligations and permit him to act. If the Prime Minister will take this course and ask the members of the House of Commons to give him the release he seeks, I for one will vote and call on my fellow members to vote to relieve him of his obligation with respect to that one specific thing.

It would be unfortunate, I think, if we lost the advantage of the extra day to the committee to consider the matter.

I cannot refuse anything
to my leader except in a matter of this importance. I was about to speak on the second reading, but a colleague was talking to me, and I had thought that the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) was to speak longer than he did. But I do not intend to speak at length, and if I am the only speaker on this matter the bill could be referred to-morrow afternoon to the committee.
May I say further that this is the most important bill which has been brought before the house for a long time. I appreciate what has been done, but it is impossible for me to refrain from saying what I have to say. I shall try to be just as brief as possible. It is not ill-will, it is not a bad disposition, but the matter is so serious that I cannot do otherwise. Besides this, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said that his intention was not to take advantage of the plebiscite right away to impose conscription, that it might be a matter of a few months, even a year, or more than that. I do not wish to be disobliging, but I should be remiss in my duty if I did not say what I have to say upon the matter. I usually refuse nothing, either to my colleagues here or to my confreres at
the bar. But this matter is of the utmost importance; we must think deeply upon it, and we have the right to express our views.
I do not wish to stand in the way, but since the bill is to be referred in the first place not to the committee of the whole house, but to a special committee which will report to the committee of the whole, it is my intention to say what I have to say in order that the members of the special committee which will study the bill will consider it, or throw it in the wastepaper basket. Mr. Speaker, will you please call it eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is not on the merits of the bill; the question is on the expediency of creating a committee to which the bill may be referred. Therefore, if any hon. member desires to speak on the motion which is now before the house, namely the expediency of creating a committee to which the bill may be referred, now is the time. Or, is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

It is one minute to eleven-o'clock, but I will continue. I started at five minutes to eleven. Sir, this is exactly the same case as when the motion was made for the reference of certain matters to the civil service committee. There was a debate on that, and hon. members expressed their views. This is not a long bill, it is a short bill. But it is based'-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I rise to a point of order. Perhaps my hon. friend will excuse me. I should like to ask Your Honour whether a motion to refer a bill to committee is debatable under the rules of the house. I would1 cite standing order 38.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does any hon. member desire to speak on the point of order?
Sir, it is now eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not yet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Standing order 38 enumerates the debatable questions. The motion to refer a bill to a committee is not therein enumerated. Therefore I declare that the motion is not debatable.
Motion agreed to.
Mr. Speaker, I move that Bill No. 10 be referred to the special committee which is now created.

Motion agreed to.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Privilege-Mr. Pouliot
Friday, February 27, 1942
